title: In Good Company — Sir Paul Marshall: Why Markets Are Getting More Competitive | Podcast | In Good Company
text: Sir Paul Marshall (Marshall Wace) — Research Memo Thesis Marshall Wace's founder argues AI is the defining capitalist event since the steam engine, that AI-linked equities (semis, Korea) remain historically cheap and not yet in bubble territory, and that durable human edge in markets has shifted from information to judgment/situational awareness — but he explicitly hedges that edge as temporary ("yet"), not permanent. Key Points Marshall Wace's franchise rests on two claims of distinctiveness: originating Alpha Capture (TOPS) and successfully fusing discretionary + systematic investing as synergistic, not competing, disciplines. AI roadmap at the firm: internal "nowcasting" (earnings/positioning signal generation) is becoming commoditized — his head of tech projects scaling from ~200 quant researchers to the equivalent of 10,000 AI agents via recursive self-improvement, expected within 6–12 months. Valuation call: US semi index at a 5–10yr low (on some measures) and Korean market at an all-time low valuation — his argument that AI-adjacent equities have moved "only in line with earnings, if that," implying room to re-rate before overheating. Bubble framework (three preconditions, none yet fully met): low rates encouraging speculation, extended valuations, unsustainable leverage. He cites the Korean leveraged-ETF market ($60B→$20B in five weeks) as a leverage-driven bubble episode that already fired and partially corrected — a real-time example of his own framework in action. Named tail-risk signpost: GPU-compute deals (e.g., Nvidia's ~$500M-scale deal) getting securitized into leveraged, CDO-like structures would mark 2007–08-style excess; not observed yet. Macro call: AI is near-term mildly inflationary (chip/energy demand) — a view he explicitly labels as consensus, not his own edge — with disinflationary productivity effects and entry-level labor-market weakness expected in 6–24 months (already visible anecdotally in UK universities), which he expects to be bullish for equities via reduced rate pressure. Firm-level counter-narrative: headcount (~750, ~200+ in tech) has been stable for two years despite heavy AI adoption; only 1 of 15 fundamental teams cut headcount. He frames AI as raising output per person, not reducing headcount — though this is his firm's specific experience, not a market-wide claim, and sits in tension with his macro entry-level-labor-weakness forecast. On market efficiency: information edge has eroded (data processing is commoditized across good firms), but he states genuine uncertainty — not salesmanship — about whether markets get more efficient overall, since rising AI-empowered retail participation may keep markets structurally inefficient (retail lacks institutional risk discipline). Structural view on shorting: mechanically harder than longs (position-sizing works against you as it moves against you; borrow costs reflect informed competition; ecosystem incentives favor bullish coverage) — he says he personally enjoys shorting despite this. Firm history: 2008 AUM fell from $14B to $3.5B not from underperformance but because its fund-of-funds-heavy client base created forced redemptions; competitors gated (he says without real liquidity justification) while Marshall Wace did not — a claim worth treating as self-reported and unverified in the transcript. Talent/hiring pivot: recruiting for traits (agency, curiosity, "disagreeableness" — civil willingness to challenge consensus) over university credentials, on the view that AI devalues exam-passing/memorization skills. Media/political footprint (relevant to key-person and reputational risk): owns/co-invests in the Spectator, GB News, and Unherd; was a Brexit financier who now says he was "wrong on the economics" but believes he was right on sovereignty, contingent on deregulation the UK hasn't delivered. Best Quotes "AI, artificial intelligence, is the most important thing that's happened in Europe, arguably in the history of capitalism." — Marshall's top-level conviction framing his entire positioning. "The semi-index in the US is at a 5- or 10-year low depending on how you look at it. The Korean market is at an all-time low valuation." — A specific, checkable valuation claim underpinning his "not yet a bubble" call. "It's gone from $60 billion of leveraged ETFs down to 20 in the last five weeks." — Concrete, quantified mechanism behind the recent Korea/momentum unwind; a template for spotting leverage-driven bubble pockets. "I'm not at all clear whether it's going to get more efficient over the next years." — Genuine epistemic humility on his own industry's central existential question, despite commercial incentive to argue markets stay exploitable. Disagreements & Conviction Efficiency of markets, going forward : Genuinely undecided (his words, not hedging for effect) — rising AI-empowered but less risk-disciplined retail flow could keep markets inefficient even as information edge disappears. Moderate-to-high intellectual honesty signal. "Not a bubble yet" vs. already-observed bubble mechanics : High conviction on valuation (cheap semis/Korea), but he simultaneously describes a leverage-driven bubble-and-correction (Korean ETFs) and a named future bubble marker (GPU-deal securitization) without reconciling why the system as a whole isn't already bubble-adjacent. He declines to time the top ("I wouldn't want to predict that"). Firm headcount stability vs. macro entry-level labor call : Confidently states Marshall Wace isn't cutting headcount from AI, while separately forecasting broad entry-level labor weakness within 6–24 months — an unreconciled tension between firm-level exceptionalism and macro-level prediction (presumably because MW is unusually selective, but he doesn't make that argument explicitly). title: Invest Like the Best — Ex-NVIDIA Engineer: Why AI Is About to Get 1000x Cheaper
text: Soul Research: Betting the Future of Inference Is Cheap, Slow, and Unattended — Research Memo Thesis Soul Research (founder Neel, ex-NVIDIA GPU kernel engineer) is building a low-cost token factory for long-horizon, background agentic workloads by deliberately abandoning the low-latency/NVLink-optimized playbook that dominates today's inference market (Fireworks, Together, BaseTen) in favor of throughput-optimized batching, "scavenged" heterogeneous chips, and distributed low-redundancy data centers. The thesis is coherent and the mechanism is real, but it rests on an unverified forecast (background inference hitting 90/10 share) and the founder's own admissions — that NVIDIA's rack-scale system currently wins on both latency and throughput, and that KV-cache/long-context inefficiency is unsolved — puncture two of the model's load-bearing assumptions. Key Points Business model : API + "sandboxes" (long-running agent VMs) serving open-source LLM tokens at the lowest cost in the market; optimizes for throughput, not speed ("it doesn't matter if it spits out tokens at 100 tokens/second... maybe 10 is just fine"). Core forecast : background vs. real-time inference workload mix goes from ~50/50 today to ~90/10 background within a few years — stated with conviction but unsourced/founder intuition, not measured data. Infra strategy ("scavenger strategy") : buy any chip, anywhere, any duration; pair with distributed ~1MW data centers tolerating 80–95% uptime and intermittent solar/wind power, betting fault-tolerant async agents don't need premium reliability. Biggest identified inefficiency : KV cache/attention memory is under-compressed by "an order of magnitude or two" (vs. MoE sparsity, which he views as already well-optimized at ~1% expert activation in frontier models). DeepSeek cited as making yearly order-of-magnitude progress here. Data/training regime shift : internet pretraining data is a "one-time subsidy," largely exhausted (~30T high-quality tokens, seen many times over); next scaling input is verifiable RL "gym" environments (coding, math, cybersecurity, agentic tasks). Explicitly scoped to verifiable problems only — human taste/quality of writing/art is excluded ("we leave the quality of writing, the beauty of art, to people"). Cost trajectory claim : a trillion-token task (~$5M at frontier API pricing today) is heading toward tens of thousands of dollars; a "definitive answer to any scientific question" toward hundreds/tens of dollars — but scoped to verifiable domains only. Contrarian chip/geopolitics view : performance-per-watt gains from Hopper→Blackwell→Rubin and across TSMC 5nm→2nm have been modest; losing TSMC access "wouldn't be that bad" since Intel is "at worst maybe 2x worse" — a specific, evidence-referenced claim, not vibes, but still one person's read. Memory/HBM as the real bottleneck : DRAM capacity discipline (Micron/SK Hynix/Samsung "burned" by past cyclicality, capex-shy) is the binding constraint — more so than TSMC wafer capacity — with the market response likely to be higher end-product prices (iPhones) and architectural workarounds (KV-cache offload to flash), not new fabs. NVIDIA's own position : doesn't compete downstream into token-selling because it profits more from a diverse, competing ecosystem of neoclouds (keeps buyers from vertically integrating away). Self-disclosed limits/caveats the guest volunteers (important for calibrating conviction): NVIDIA's NVL72 rack currently offers both best latency and best throughput — undercutting the clean latency-vs-throughput dichotomy used to justify Soul's positioning. Software/kernel efficiency edge is explicitly non-durable: "we're all downstream of the frontier... the rising tide... lifts all boats." KV cache/long-context remains an unsolved "thorn"; he personally uses /compact in Claude Code well before 1M context, implying labs' long-context claims outpace real usability. Best Quotes "We're going to end this year at maybe 50/50 background and real-time workloads, but I see this going to 90/10 in favor of background." — Guest. Core, testable TAM assumption for the entire business; unanchored to data. "My contrarian take is that it wouldn't be that bad [losing TSMC access]... Intel—not that far behind, at worst maybe 2x worse performance per watt." — Guest. Non-consensus, mechanism-grounded view that could reprice Taiwan tail-risk premium in semis. "I'm cool with that... my customers don't care because their agent was running for hours... our P99 latency, it's not going to be controlled. It cannot be. And in return, I'll give you unbeatable economics." — Guest. The actual mechanism behind Soul's cost advantage — distributed, low-redundancy infra — and its risk. "The rising tide of something like Mythos or GPT-5.6 Soul that lifts all boats... I actually don't think there's a point in specializing... we're all downstream of the frontier." — Guest. Guest's own admission that the software/kernel-efficiency edge (a stated pillar of the company) is not a durable moat. Disagreements & Conviction Latency vs. throughput as the defining infra bet (guest vs. incumbents): high conviction, stated as directional certainty ("very obvious"). But internally inconsistent — he separately concedes NVIDIA's NVL72 currently wins on both axes, meaning his own flagship justification for de-prioritizing NVLink is undercut by his own words. Treat the dichotomy as strategic positioning, not settled fact. 90/10 background-workload forecast : medium-low conviction — reads as founder intuition/aspiration ("I love this market because it's unbounded"), not measured. He does offer a supporting anecdote (he's personally capped on real-time token consumption at Codex/Claude Code), which mildly strengthens the case for real-time demand being bounded, but the 90/10 figure itself is unsupported. TSMC/geopolitical risk overstated : genuinely non-consensus and evidence-referenced (specific perf/watt comparisons across chip generations), not merely

title: joseph_carlson — I’m Buying $10,000 Of This Company Next
text: Buy-the-Dip Roulette, the Uber Pricing Backlash, and the Munster/Meta Call — Research Memo Thesis Joseph (solo creator, ~$1.5M live portfolio, 14.8% time-weighted CAGR) is running a rules-based dip-buying mechanic that pre-commits $10K to whichever of 14 mega-cap/quality holdings first hits a preset trigger 18–47% below its current price — a discipline device more than a valuation call. The episode's more transferable signal is his contrarian read on two live sentiment risks: he argues Uber's "personalized pricing" media firestorm is a mischaracterized dynamic-pricing story, and he argues Gene Munster's Meta bear call is a repeat of Munster's previously-wrong Google/ChatGPT bearishness — in both cases betting that a loud negative narrative is already priced in or factually overstated. Key Points Mechanic : $10K in fresh cash auto-deploys to whichever of 14 holdings first hits its buy target; targets are 18–25% below current price for most names, but 38% (Costco: $600 vs. $969) and 47% (DoorDash: $120) for two. Full target list w/ host's own implied 5-yr CAGR (his DCF, "conservative" assumptions): Google $250 (14.1%), Mastercard $450 (18.5%), Amazon $200 (19.3%), Meta $450 (17.2%), S&P Global $350 (~16%), ASML $1,200 (15.2%), Netflix $60 (19.9%), Microsoft $400 (16.8%), Costco $600 (10.6%), Texas Roadhouse $140 (13.4%), Moody's $375 (12.1%), Duolingo $90 (14.2%), DoorDash $120 (15%), Uber $60 (20.9%). Notable clustering : every one of the 12+ "conservative" scenarios lands 10.6–20.9% CAGR — a suspiciously narrow, uniformly favorable band across unrelated sectors (payments, cloud/ads, streaming, ratings agencies, ride-share). Reads more like scenario-justification for prices already chosen than independent valuation (inference, not stated by host). Portfolio stats : $1.5M value, +$540K total gain, +1.5%/$22K since Aug 21 episode, 14.8% time-weighted CAGR since inception (vs. a hypothetical ~$3M/$2M gain if all capital had been deployed on day one — illustrating most deposits came late and haven't compounded as long). Falsifiable call : host believes it's likely at least one of the 14 triggers within 6 months, reasoning from portfolio-level odds even though each individual trigger is called "unlikely" in isolation. Caveat (inference): these are correlated large-cap/quality-growth names, so the most probable trigger path is a systemic drawdown hitting several at once — not idiosyncratic single-name weakness — which slightly overstates the diversification logic. Uber pricing controversy : More Perfect Union and Business Insider both released viral (hundreds of thousands of views) videos alleging Uber uses "personalized/surveillance pricing," based on same-route trips priced differently among riders requesting simultaneously. Uber's technical rebuttal (quoted at length by host): fares are trip-specific (time, demand, driver availability, traffic) not person-specific, and Uber states on record it does not use protected characteristics, phone battery/model, or behavioral segments to price. Host argues both outlets omitted Uber's rebuttal — "massive omission bias," not journalism. Munster/Meta : Gene Munster (Deepwater Asset Management, discloses no position in Meta) calls current teen-safety litigation "the tip of the iceberg," estimates ~$25B in Meta fines over 5 years (against $40-60B/yr steady-state cash flow — he concedes affordability), and projects "dramatically bigger" future lawsuits tied to Zuckerberg's "superbot" pivot announced Aug 10. He opens by explicitly disclaiming he's "a big believer in AI" long-term — a hedge the host's framing does not carry forward. Host's rebuttal to Munster : rests entirely on track record — Munster was similarly structurally bearish on Google pre-ChatGPT near $170 (Google since ~doubled, Munster now owns it and is bullish). Host notes Meta trades at 18x forward PE with lawsuits "already well known" and calls this "fail of the week," while explicitly hedging: "Maybe Gene will be right this time." Best Quotes "That is dynamic pricing. That is not personal pricing. And that's an important detail." — Host. Crux of his Uber rebuttal; distinguishes trip-level real-time pricing from individual profiling. "To be clear, Uber does not engage in surveillance pricing... we do not use protected characteristics, phone battery levels, phone models, or other devices or information to set prices." — Host, quoting Uber's official statement. The company's on-record denial underpinning the whole rebuttal — note the host does not independently verify this, he accepts Uber's self-published explanation at face value. "Before I need to preface my comments that I'm a big believer in AI... but I think what we're seeing here around the courts is minimal — I think it is the tip of the iceberg... probably lawsuits that are dramatically bigger." — Gene Munster. His actual framing opens AI-bullish, then pivots to legal-liability-bearish on Meta specifically — a nuance the host's "fail of the week" framing elides. "Meta is trading at an 18 forward PE. Investors already know about the lawsuits... this is an incredibly powerful company with terrible sentiment already priced into the stock." — Host. His explicit sentiment-vs-fundamentals variant view on Meta. Disagreements & Conviction Host vs. Munster on Meta : High conviction, explicit ("Gene, you're just doing it again, man"), built entirely on track-record pattern-matching (Munster's prior wrong Google call), not fresh fundamental analysis. Genuinely hedged at the close: "Maybe Gene will be right this time... I don't believe that's typically how it happens." Note: Munster/Deepwater disclosed no position in Meta — a fact present in the transcript's CNBC intro but never invoked by the host himself; treat any "skin-in-the-game" framing as reader inference, not the host's argument. Host vs. activist/media narrative on Uber : Very high conviction, stated as fact rather than opinion ("this is not what journalism looks like"). Source-quality

title: meb_faber — Why Trend Following Feels Wrong (But Could Boost Your Portfolio)
text: Trend Following After a Rough 2025: Jerry Parker on Why "Managed Futures" Isn't Trend Following — Research Memo Thesis Jerry Parker (Chesapeake Capital/MFUT) argues that pure, unsmoothed, stock-inclusive trend following is a distinct and structurally under-owned strategy — diluted by most "managed futures" peers via mean-reversion/carry blending and crisis-alpha positioning — and that institutional re-allocation to it is gated purely on a stretch of relative outperformance vs. equities, not on any structural or narrative catalyst. Key Points Parker distinguishes "managed futures"/CTA (the SocGen index category) from pure trend following: CTAs now blend in mean reversion, carry, pattern recognition, short-term trading, AI — "maybe 50%, 75% for some" trend exposure — versus "100% for MFUT and Chesapeake." Implication: SocGen CTA Index performance is not a clean proxy for pure trend returns. Pure trend win rate is ~40% or less; 5-10% of trades generate all the returns, relying on small, consistent loss-cutting plus unconstrained profit-running on winners. Parker rejects "crisis alpha" as the primary CTA value proposition, calling client demand for it "almost a Stockholm syndrome." He claims some managers deliberately design worse-performing, crash-correlated products to justify allocations — a self-described non-consensus, pointed critique of industry peers. Chesapeake/MFUT trades individual single-name stocks (e.g., Newmont, Lockheed, Merck), long and short, arguing index-level trading (S&P, EFA, EEM) mutes the outlier moves trend depends on. He also acknowledges the flip side: stocks can desync less than expected and "kick our butt" for extended periods, and recent gains are concentrated in the "best performing trending group of the past 10-20 years" (stocks) — a self-flagged, unresolved tension. Portfolio construction at Chesapeake is deliberately non-optimized: equal allocation across currencies, commodities, stocks, rates; minimal backtesting/overweighting; and deliberate holding of highly correlated pairs (gold/silver, crude/heating oil) to avoid missing one-sided outlier events (cites silver's 1987 spike vs. gold's smaller move). Risk discipline: cut losses fast and consistently, but explicitly refuse to dampen volatility on winning trades — Parker states backtests show smoothing/vol-targeting mechanically destroys the right-tail outliers that fund the whole strategy. April 2025 example: "the whole portfolio can become highly correlated... we lost money on everything" — a direct, transcript-stated admission that trend's diversification benefit is regime-dependent, not constant, and can fail exactly during macro-shock stress. Performance framing: the SocGen Trend Index had a rough/possibly worst-ever 12-month stretch in the period the host calls "last year," while the year in which this podcast was recorded has been comparably strong; within that, 2025 specifically was discussed as down only ~1-2% — Parker frames this as normal cyclicality (process over performance), not evidence of a broken strategy. Note: the transcript never specifies calendar years for the "rough" stretch beyond "last year" vs. "this year" — treat any specific year label as inference, not transcript fact. Forward-looking, falsifiable claim: Parker predicts a "born-again" institutional re-embrace of trend once it next delivers better relative performance vs. equities — no other adoption catalyst is invoked. Host's framing: typical advisor portfolios are 80-100% US equities with no ex-US or real-asset exposure; trend is pitched not just as left-tail crisis protection but as right-tail exposure to under-owned assets (gold, silver, commodities, ex-US equities) — though Parker notes gold and silver are "sinking" as of the taping, so this right-tail case is thesis, not a present-tense trend signal. Host states the "honest," bias-free allocation a quant/CIO would choose is ~25% to trend, versus a typical real-world allocation of 0-5%; the host's own strategic allocation is 50%, described as a significant outlier. Best Quotes "It used to be 100% for all the CTAs. Now it's maybe a lot less than that, maybe 50%, 75% for some, 100% for MFUT and Chesapeake." — Jerry Parker. Core differentiation claim underlying the entire product thesis. "Some CTAs have even gone that route and said I'm going to choose worse performance for my fund, my livelihood, my family, my trend following loving clients because I'll be able to convince others that I need a big allocation... even though my overall performance will be worse and my fee income will be less possibly." — Jerry Parker. Pointed, non-consensus accusation about peer incentive misalignment — directly relevant to manager selection. "The whole portfolio can become highly correlated like we saw in April of '25 where we lost money on everything." — Jerry Parker. Direct admission that trend's diversification benefit is regime-dependent and can fail during the exact stress periods it's marketed to protect against. "There is no strategy available with a large sample size that you could backtest and confirm that it actually worked that tried to sell silver at those levels... This particular trade, the one that you're most concerned with, I have no clue how to do that." — Jerry Parker. Candid admission of a structural blind spot (no edge calling tops) — sets realistic expectations for the strategy's failure modes. Disagreements & Conviction Managed futures ≠ trend following (Parker vs. industry usage): High conviction, but self-flagged as opinion/overstatement ("this is my opinion and I don't have anyone to debate... to set me straight"; admits his tweets are deliberate provocations). Material for allocators: don't treat SocGen CTA index as a pure-trend proxy. Crisis alpha as the sell point (Parker vs. consensus advisor/allocator framing): Very high conviction, sustained and specific ("Stockholm syndrome," "silly situation"). Genuinely non-consensus relative to how CTAs are typically market

title: algys_investment_podcast — Jack Barrat: Why UK Stocks May Offer Compelling Value Right Now | #28
text: Jack Barrett (Man GLG) — Research Memo Thesis Barrett runs a UK-focused (small European sleeve) long-short capital-cycle value strategy, and is maximally positioned in unloved, tangible-asset-heavy cyclicals (paper/packaging, industrial engineers, steel refractories, aggregates, bricks, housebuilders) trading at one-in-10-to-20-year valuation lows — a trade whose payoff depends on trough-to-mid-cycle earnings normalization and is structurally short a return to zero-cost-of-capital conditions. Conviction is high and process-driven, but Barrett himself bounds the call to a multi-year (not 10-year) horizon and explicitly disclaims being a catalyst investor, so timing is unspecified. Key Points Process: not classic screening (P/E, yield) but capital-cycle analysis of tangible-asset cash returns vs. price paid ("pages 180–320 of an annual report"). Current largest overweight: industrials/materials — cyclical, asset-heavy names at record/near-record valuation lows vs. normalized earnings power ("earnings double and then double again" as a stylized, not universal, case). UK opportunity set: ~two-thirds of the UK market's ~20%-odd return last year came from only 12 stocks — narrow leadership leaving a large "left-behind" tail. Capital return tailwind: over half of strategy holdings have recently bought back or are actively buying back stock; some have retired over a third of share count since COVID — a shrinking-supply technical. Mid-cap vs. large-cap: UK mid-cap index underperformed large-cap by "well over a third" over the last four years; the fund's earlier large-cap tilt was a bottom-up process output, not an index call, and it's now rotating back down-cap as opportunity re-emerges. US market: headline >20x earnings, but on a free-cash-flow basis (capex explosion) "probably the most expensive... in a long, long time" — a mechanism-based non-consensus valuation flag. 2025 was the firm's hardest year on record for Barrett personally; several "great risk-adjusted decisions" didn't pay off — an unprompted, credibility-building admission. AI: three concrete workstreams (mining historical trade write-ups for behavioral lessons; semi-agentic internal workflows used 15–20x/day; modularizing the investment process) — explicitly hedged as unproven ("moving fast and breaking things... I don't know which of these are going to work"), and current model-build time may currently be longer , not shorter, with a 40–60% reduction stated only as a future aspiration. Top macro risks named: (1) a material credit cycle (unseen since GFC) — would hurt this portfolio too in the near term before creating opportunity; (2) a return to zero-cost-of-capital/QE — the strategy's true structural Achilles heel, a multi-year headwind even as it lifts the market via a "sugar high." Explicitly declines 10-year sector forecasts as outside his "circle of competence" — bounds how far to extrapolate the cyclicals thesis. Best Quotes "Almost two-thirds of the 20-odd percent return delivered by the UK market last year was delivered by only 12 stocks." — quantifies market narrowness underpinning the UK left-behind-value thesis. "On a free cash flow basis, given the explosion in capex... it's probably the most expensive [the US market has] been in a long, long time." — non-consensus, testable valuation mechanism. "I think last year was probably the hardest year that we had... some of the great risk-adjusted decisions... didn't come off." — rare, unprompted honesty on manager track record. "The one thing we don't view or subscribe to... is the idea of risk as volatility... we don't believe risk is symmetrical... around the current share price." — core philosophical differentiator vs. mainstream risk frameworks. Disagreements & Conviction Risk ≠ volatility : explicit rejection of mainstream (vol-targeting/index) risk framework; high, process-embedded conviction, reinforced by stated book influences (Howard Marks). Cyclicals/value vs. market's growth/mega-cap tilt : maximally overweight the out-of-favor side of the market; conviction framed as validated by discomfort ("when the strategy is at its best is when you feel sort of most uncertain"). High conviction, explicitly time-bound to current market structure, not a permanent stance. AI optimism vs. self-described habitual skepticism : Barrett notes he was a correct skeptic on COVID office-return calls and blockchain, yet is unusually bullish on AI's productivity impact — flagged by him as personally uncomfortable, which lends some credibility, but results are self-admittedly unproven. "Not catalyst investors" vs. active trading around price : minor, likely semantic (patient on thesis, tactical on sizing) rather than a real contradiction — not flagged as tension by Barrett himself. Investment Implications UK breadth/left-behind value (1–3yr): passive UK exposure is effectively a 12-stock concentration story; active UK managers face prolonged tracking-error pain unless/until breadth normalizes. Affected: FTSE mid/small-cap value, UK active managers, FTSE trackers. Shrinking UK equity supply via buybacks/M&A (now–2-3yr): mechanically accretive and a positive technical, but self-liquidating — the inefficiency being harvested erodes as take-privates/buybacks continue; part of the return may effectively be a bet on being acquired before re-rating. Affected: UK small/mid-cap value, PE/strategic acquirers, LSE listing economics. Cyclical/tangible-asset trough trade (2–5yr, MODEL INFERENCE on regime-dependency): payoff is asymmetric and regime-conditional — a rates-normalization/real-economy recovery helps it, a return to easy money (Barrett's most-feared scenario) could starve it further even as growth assets re-rate. Affected: UK industrials, building materials, housebuilders, steel/aggregates; implicitly short long-duration growth factor. title: masters_in_business — Learning from Buffett and Munger | Masters in Business with Alex Morris
text: Buffett and Munger Unscripted: Lessons from 31 Years of Berkshire Meetings — Research Memo Thesis Alex Morris's exhaustive synthesis of 31 years of Berkshire annual meetings (1994–c.2025) reinforces that Buffett/Munger's edge was temperament and adaptability, not IQ or dogma — and their own biggest admitted misses (Geico/telematics, dismissing Apple) show the "circle of competence" is a moving target, not a fixed perimeter. The most actionable takeaway for a PM is behavioral: Morris's own portfolio evidence (holding Microsoft through a P/E re-rate, sizing Peloton up after a 97% drawdown) argues against mechanical valuation-driven trimming/rebalancing as a discipline — and Berkshire's own $300B+ cash pile quietly undercuts its "no macro forecasting" mythology. Key Points Temperament over IQ : Core recurring theme across 31 years — emotional stability, patience, and independence from crowd opinion drive compounding; "sell 30 points" off a 160 IQ is the host's paraphrase of a Buffett sentiment Morris affirms in substance, not a verbatim book quote. Adaptability beats dogma : Geico missed Progressive's telematics-based pricing shift for years and fell behind in scale; Buffett/Munger dismissed Apple/Google (2011-13) as "too hard" before Apple became one of Berkshire's largest-ever positions (~$200B at peak). Extreme concentration, near-zero turnover : Buffett's last Coca-Cola purchase was 1994 (once >30% of Berkshire's equity portfolio) — untouched 30+ years. Frames Morris's "only ~20 lifetime decisions matter" heuristic, which he applies to his own 10–15-name portfolio. Insurance float as the engine : Geico, Gen Re, National Indemnity float has funded Berkshire's investment/acquisition strategy for decades; Geico's telematics lag is a structural (not just competitive) drag on that engine's growth. Morris's own book : covers the archive from 1994 forward (Amazon Best Book of 2025) — roughly through 2024/2025 meetings. He separately attended the 2026 meeting (Greg Abel's first as CEO) as a personal event, outside the book's research scope. Greg Abel era : Abel (CEO since Jan 1, 2026) addresses operational problems (Geico, BNSF underperformance) directly in public Q&A, a departure from Buffett's reluctance to criticize managers by name. Buyback pace has slowed since 2019, which Morris reads as an implicit signal management sees the market as not cheap. Cash pile is "north of 300 billion"; Morris expects tens of billions, "potentially over a hundred billion," deployed in a real dislocation. Morris's live positions : Peloton (bought post-crash, $150→<$4, subs went 500K→3M→2.5M; now his largest position on a cyclical-not-structural thesis), Dollar Tree (bought H2 2024, Dollarama-replication thesis), long-held Microsoft (since 2011) and Berkshire (since 2011), exited Disney into Netflix (2022). Microsoft case study : Bought 2011 at high-single-digit ex-cash P/E; held through 2015-16 re-rate to mid-teens despite value-investor consensus to sell; stock compounded at a mid-20s% annualized return over the following decade — Morris's central argument against valuation-triggered selling of quality compounders. Best Quotes "Warren started buying in... '88 or '89. He bought his last share in '94 and he hasn't bought or sold a single share since then which is at a point in time it was more than 30% of Berkshire's equity portfolio." — Guest. Empirical anchor for the "20 lifetime decisions" concentration thesis. "Basically, Apple's too hard for us. We'll never own it." ... "Fast forward a few years, and it was... almost a $200 billion position, and it's one of the greatest investments of all time." — Guest, quoting Munger then commenting. Shows the magnitude of their own circle-of-competence reversal. "It's funny to look back now... over the last decade the stock's compounded at a mid-20s annualized return, which happens all the time with companies like this where people... become too focused on the valuation." — Guest. His core lesson against mechanical valuation-driven selling (Microsoft). "I think it's north of 300 [billion in cash]... they're willing to spend tens and tens of billions of dollars or potentially even over a hundred billion dollars at the right opportunities... I'm sure the day will come where things look really ugly." — Guest. Forward-looking read on Berkshire's dry powder under Abel. Disagreements & Conviction Peloton vs. "structural decline" consensus — High conviction, backed by actual sizing (now his largest position), not just talk. Analogized to mattresses (pandemic-boom category still below peak but not "dead"). Morris concedes cost-structure/execution problems are real, tempering the bull case. Valuation-triggered selling vs. traditional value-investing consensus — High conviction, explicit: calls IRR/valuation-driven trimming "a flawed way to do things." Generalizes his own Microsoft experience into a standing rule. Berkshire's "no macro forecasting" claim vs. its $300B+ cash pile — Genuinely unresolved; Morris raises the contradiction himself ("wonder how much of that is... maybe not a macro forecast") then partially retreats to "all the micro is the macro." Honest ambivalence, not a hedge for effect — flagged as low-conviction/open in the QA audit. Munger's own influence on Buffett — Buffett credits Munger with shifting him from cigar-butt to quality-business investing; Munger himself downplays it. Morris explicitly declines to adjudicate ("you got to pick which one you want to agree with or believe"). Low stakes, but flags that the "buy wonderful businesses" origin story is contested even by its authors. Buffett's 2008 "Buy America" op-ed — Host frames it as a good macro call; Morris pushes back ("it was down another 30% six months later... my timing wasn't particularly great"), reframing it as valuation-driven rather than tactical market-timing. Moderate conviction, low-stakes correction. Investment Implications Peloton (PTON) — First-order: cyclical-not-structural thesis impli

title: intrinsic_value — Domino's Pizza (DPZ): Is the Royalty Engine Still Running?
text: Domino's Pizza (DPZ) — Research Memo Thesis Domino's is a capital-light franchise "royalty" business that has compounded EPS ~15%/year for two decades almost entirely via buybacks and margin mix-shift (franchise/international royalties over corporate stores), not organic growth — but revenue growth has decelerated from ~11%/year to ~3%/year since 2022, same-store sales have stalled (+0.1% US, -0.1% intl. in Q2 2026), and the business is levered ~4.8x EBITDA to fund distributions that have at times exceeded free cash flow. The episode's own guest concludes the moat is thin and takes a pass at current levels (~20x P/E, down from 40x in 2020), flagging debt structure, insider selling, and long-term health-trend risk as reasons for caution. Key Points World's largest pizza chain: ~22,300+ locations, 90 markets; ~99% franchised; US segment ~33% of revenue (~7,000 franchised + ~186 corporate stores, down from 375 in 2022). Segment EBIT margins vary widely: supply chain (~60% of revenue) 10%; US stores 36%; international franchise (zero corporate stores) 85% — blending to ~21% overall EBIT margin on ~$5B revenue. ROIC runs ~100% but this is largely a denominator effect: NOPAT compounded only 4.2% (2021–2025) while invested capital shrank via corporate-store divestiture — not a genuine profitability improvement. Equity is -$4B; funded via debt-heavy shareholder distributions. In 2022, buybacks ($1.32B) + dividends ($139M) exceeded operating cash flow ($650M). Financing is via whole-business securitization (royalty/IP/supply-chain cash flows pledged as collateral) at a low 3.82% blended coupon — cheaper than conventional debt, but creditors hold priority claims on cash release. Long-term debt ~$4.8B vs. ~$1B EBITDA; covenant ceiling 5.5x debt/EBITDA. Franchisee alignment mechanism (previously omitted, now confirmed important): Domino's shares ~50% of supply-chain operating income with franchises that purchase from its supply centers — voluntary but near-universal, and a direct structural defense against a Quiznos-style franchisee revolt. "Fortressing" — deliberately clustering stores close together (rather than spacing to avoid cannibalization) to improve delivery speed/freshness and carryout convenience — is a genuine, non-obvious company-specific strategy, now being extended internationally. Growth levers going forward: aggregator (Uber/DoorDash) expansion (~$1B incremental revenue estimate vs. $5B base), rewards program (36M members), and international store growth (unit count +6%/year since 2012); US market considered largely saturated. Over half a dozen publicly traded Domino's master franchises exist internationally (Jubilant Foodworks–India, DPC Dash–China/HK, Domino's Pizza Group–UK) — a direct read-through/comp set not otherwise covered by US-centric analysis. Franchisee unit economics: Domino's avg. store revenue ~$1.4M vs. Pizza Hut ~$1M; ~$165K EBITDA/store; 4–6 year payback on ~$500K investment — supports why Domino's wins franchisee mindshare over rivals. Management comp tied to adjusted EBITDA growth (10%/yr target) and relative TSR vs. a restaurant subindex — not EPS; insider ownership <1%; no open-market insider buys in 2 years despite two 30%+ drawdowns (current: -39%). Berkshire Hathaway held ~10% of DPZ, fully exited in early 2026. Guest's valuation: base case 5.5% revenue growth, ~20.5% EBITDA margin, 17x EV/EBITDA, 20% margin of safety → ~$383/share fair value. Note: transcript never states DPZ's current share price, so whether $383 implies over/undervaluation cannot be confirmed from the episode alone. Best Quotes "So net operating profits after tax or NOPAT... has been compounding at only 4.2% between 2021 and 2025. So this return on invested capital is being propped up by other changes in its invested capital base." — Guest. Exposes the ~100% ROIC as a shrinking-denominator artifact, not real profit growth. "If we go back to 2022, they repurchased shares worth $1.32 billion while generating $650 million in operating cash flow... you can see where I get a little uneasy here." — Guest. Concrete evidence distributions have outpaced free cash flow, funded by debt. "I'm hesitant to say that this business won't be around in the next 2 years. But if I look out maybe 20 years from now, I would say I have zero conviction in saying that this business will still be around." — Guest. The episode's starkest, most non-consensus durability call, driven by GLP-1/health-trend risk. "Yeah, if we could get at like eight times earnings, I would look at it, but not so much today." — Host (only; not endorsed by guest in transcript). An explicit, actionable re-entry bogey roughly 60% below the current ~20x multiple. Disagreements & Conviction Moat skepticism (high conviction, guest): Guest repeatedly downgrades every operational strength (aggregator deals, delivery ownership, brand) to "some sort of advantage" rather than a true moat, concluding plainly he "still don't think I would be comfortable with it given the scale." Host is milder, crediting brand/execution more — a soft tension, not a hard clash. Internal tension in guest's own analysis: His base-case DCF outputs ~$383 (via a 17x EV/EBITDA multiple, which is not obviously consistent with a "no moat" thesis), yet he closes by passing entirely — his real decision appears driven by qualitative risk (GLP-1s, debt structure, weak insider buying) rather than the model output. Caveat (corrected from earlier draft): the guest never states his own numeric reservation price; the 8x-earnings bogey is the host's alone, not "echoed approvingly" by the guest — treat that figure as one analyst's view, not a shared conviction price. Securitization structure — genuine unresolved ambivalence: Guest calls the low 3.82% coupon "brilliant" financing but also flags it as ceding cash-flow control to creditors; host treats it as an outright red flag ("management not having full discretion over the business's cash"). This is convergent skepticism, not real disa

title: core_finance — An Introduction to Vesari, Inc
text: Viridis (Vasari/Basalt) Geothermal-Powered AI Compute — Research Memo Thesis Viridis is pitching a behind-the-meter geothermal-to-AI-compute business — selling tokens per second instead of electricity — but every economic figure in the deck (the $293M IP valuation, the $350M/facility revenue projection, the 16–20% IRR) rests on management-authored assumptions with no signed land, permits, or off-take agreements yet in place. This is a pre-revenue narrative-and-comps story (explicitly modeled on Fervo's IPO), not yet an operating thesis. Key Points Business model : co-locate 100MW geothermal plants with hyperscale data centers, monetizing compute ("200 to 250 million tokens per second" per plant) rather than power, with LEO satellite (Starlink/Kuiper-type) uplink/downlink replacing fiber for remote siting. Efficiency claim : management estimates 23–36% greater efficiency than any existing geothermally-powered hyperscaler, built from four IP-layer estimates (site integration 6–9%, cooling/waste-heat 12–18%, orchestration 10–16%, remote/CFE certification 5–9%) and a targeted PUE of 1.1–1.18 vs. an industry-average 1.56 — all company-estimated ("we reckon," "we estimate"), with no third-party validation and unclear additivity across differing bases. IP valuation : 11 utility patents (filed June 2026, grant status not stated) valued at $293M by Cardinal IP via DCF; auditors reviewed methodology under IFRS 13. Critically, the CFO discloses the DCF uses management's own revenue projections — only the discount rate and royalty comps are independently sourced. The "independent" label applies to methodology/pricing inputs, not to the demand/volume assumptions driving the number. Unit economics (per 100MW facility, management estimate) : ~$350M average annual revenue, ~$220M opex, ~$130M EBITDA (37% margin), 16–20% unlevered IRR — built on $150–180/kW-month market lease rates (CBRE/JLL-sourced) plus a self-selected 20% midpoint "24/7 carbon-free energy premium" (stated range 10–30%). Milestones (falsifiable, dated) : investment bank onboarding targeted end of August 2026; BLM parcel bids targeted October 2026; site control targeted by end of 2026; SPAC/reverse-merger process "under consideration," planned concurrently with — not after — the anchor hyperscaler off-take. Comp used to justify valuation : Fervo's IPO — "$135,000 in revenue in 2025," raised "over $2 billion," market cap "over $7 billion" — cited as precedent that pre-revenue geothermal off-take models command large valuations. Transcript gives no detail on Fervo's operational/construction status beyond these figures. Unaddressed/thin risk areas : no discussion of drilling/execution risk, capex financing terms, or water rights; competitive moat is asserted only in one unsubstantiated line ("we don't believe rivals will be able to easily match"); no mention of any actual contract with Starlink/Kuiper despite dependence on their network. Best Quotes "We're not selling a single watt of the electricity we will be geothermally generating... We're going to use all those watts in our campus to sell compute or tokens per second." (host) — defines the entire valuation pivot from power seller to compute seller. "It came back at actually $293 million as of the end of June." (host) — the headline IP valuation now sitting on the H1 balance sheet, pre-revenue and pre-construction. "They had $135,000 in revenue in 2025, and they raised over $2 billion in the last 3 months. And their market cap is over $7 billion." (host) — the valuation anchor for the whole pitch; flags a sector-wide willingness to price geothermal-for-AI narratives far ahead of fundamentals. "Both are referenced to observable market pricing rather than our own assumptions... this is not a Fervo forecast." (guest, Dubrawsky) — a preemptive defense of revenue inputs that signals the CFO expects this to be the diligence battleground. Disagreements & Conviction No adversarial exchange exists in the transcript — host and CFO are fully aligned; this is a solo-narrated pitch. The real tensions are internal: - "We sell tokens, not power" branding vs. power-denominated economics : the entire revenue model is priced in $/kW-month plus a power premium — the "tokens" framing looks like positioning to support a tech/IP valuation multiple rather than a power-generation multiple. High rhetorical conviction, thin operational distinction. - "No public comparable" vs. citing Fervo as direct precedent : Gross states he's "quite confident" there's no comparable, then in the same breath uses Fervo's off-take-driven, pre-revenue IPO as the model to justify Vasari's strategy — internally inconsistent, reads as promotional inflation rather than genuine differentiation. - "Independent" IP valuation vs. company-supplied inputs : methodology and comps are third-party-sourced, but the demand/volume forecast (the main driver of a DCF) is management's own — a materially weaker claim than "independent valuation" implies. The CFO's own candor here is the strongest signal of where scrutiny will land. - Precision vs. rigor in efficiency stack : four ranges hedged with "we reckon" are summed into a confident 23–36% headline with no stated methodology for additivity across different bases — likely a simplification, not a rigorously derived output. Investment Implications First-order : A pre-revenue, pre-permit company books a $293M fair-value IP asset on its balance sheet, materially inflating reported NAV ahead of any operating milestone (immediate, H1 2026 reporting). Second-order (inference) : If a SPAC/reverse-merger proceeds using this valuation and the Fervo comp as pricing anchors, public/late-stage capital could be raised before the anchor hyperscaler off-take — the one event that would validate the revenue assumptions — is signed. The transcript explicitly sequences capital-raising concurrently with, not after, the anchor off-take, creating a window where investors underwrite a model, not a contracted revenue s

title: made_in_japan — Ep.4: How to invest in Japanese growth stocks with Praveen Kumar
text: Japan Growth Investing: The Culture-Not-Language Edge — Research Memo Guest: Pina, ex-Baillie Gifford Japanese equities analyst/co-PM (~15-16 years covering Japan; formerly co-managed a ~$1.5B all-cap strategy and sole-led a ~$700-750M Japan small-cap strategy) Thesis Japan should be analyzed with the same fundamental growth-investing framework used anywhere else, but foreign investors persistently misprice it by clinging to outdated "deflation/debt/demographics" narratives and overweighting language ability over cultural fluency and on-the-ground fieldwork. Her structural view: Japan rarely mints 10-30x multibaggers (business models are margin-expansion-driven, not top-line compounders), so the repeatable edge is finding 3-5x margin-expansion stories early and having the discipline to exit before the market "gets onto the story." Key Points Language vs. culture: Japanese fluency provides no analytical edge (translators suffice); understanding cultural context — e.g., why firms avoid layoffs, how to phrase management questions non-confrontationally — is the real differentiator. Framed language expertise as a "comfort blanket" for investors, not a genuine moat. Decoupling from macro: Explicit filter — avoid companies "that rely on some external factor going their way... they live and die by their own decisions." Economic growth and stock returns are only weakly correlated (her view, citing unspecified "numerous academic studies"). Return distribution in Japan: Structural growth stories (10-15% top-line, margin gains — e.g., M3, GMO Payment Gateway) are rare; the more common opportunity is pure margin-expansion re-rating, yielding frequent 3-5x rather than 10x+ winners. Concrete case: SWCC Showa (5805) bought at 4-5x P/E with low-single-digit operating margins in 2022, now ~10-11% margins, re-rated to ~20x P/E — a 6-7x return. Sell discipline: "You should not overstay your welcome" — Japan's narrower multiple ceiling means rapid harvesting/trimming, not buy-and-hold (explicitly contrasted with US/Fastenal-style and India/Pulak Prasad-style never-sell approaches). Reconciled with Baillie Gifford's long-term brand via former boss Sarah Whitley's framing: "if you came into the office one morning and found the world had changed, it would be odd for your portfolio not to." Edge = business-model uniqueness , not tech/patents/first-mover advantage, given how fast Japanese competitors replicate any perceived edge. Examples: Infomart (~¥2T GMV, built on Japan's fax-based food-ordering norms), Bengo4.com (online legal), Cosmos Pharmaceutical (organic everyday-low-price retail, zero M&A). Management/ownership screen: Strong bias toward founder-led businesses (~90% of her former holdings) because Japanese executive pay is low, so insider ownership is otherwise structurally weak. Also flags outsider-CEO turnarounds (Shiseido's Uotani, ex-Coca-Cola Japan) as a positive signal. Portfolio construction/risk data point: Internal research team found evidence of a market-cap "ceiling" around ¥100bn where Japanese small/mid-caps struggle to break through to the next stage (30→50→100bn is easy; 100→200bn is hard) — a quantitative, actionable input for position-sizing and exit timing. Valuation methodology: Moved from DCF/reverse-DCF to EV/EBIT as primary tool — EV captures Japan's often-ignored large net-cash balances; EBIT (vs. P/E or net income) avoids distortion from Japan's "recurring profit" and below-the-line items. Not used for pre-profit SaaS names (price/sales instead). Japan SaaS dispersion view: Bearish on horizontal/mainstream players (Freee, Money Forward) — "jam tomorrow" stories vulnerable to Japan's unusually fast competitive entry; bullish on vertical-niche, relationship-moat names (Cybozu/Kintone targeting local government, Infomart, Bengo4.com). Katitas (8919) thesis: Renovates abandoned houses ( akiya ) for first-time buyers; ~8 million empty homes nationally and growing (not a static/depleting TAM), rising rates make renovated-house mortgages cheaper than rent, and municipalities now proactively refer inventory to Katitas as competitors have exited the operationally hard niche — expects ~10-12% earnings growth for a long period, not a static discount to the space. SoftBank thesis: Former ~9% position in her all-cap fund, biggest contributor to trailing-12-month performance. Investment case reduces to "it's all about Mr. Son" (Masayoshi Son) — buy when market sentiment treats him as an "idiot," sell as it swings toward "genius." Near-term upside flagged: potential Anthropic IPO-style value-crystallization event. Forward call: Next decade favors growth over the recent value/cash-hoarding/governance-reform trade ("these are companies that have a shelf life... once value is realized, what next?"). She "senses" — her word choice is hedged — that the past decade's winners won't be the next decade's winners; flags embedded inflation, demographic pressure (healthcare automation, drugstore consolidation), and possible immigration liberalization as tailwinds for new names. Best Quotes "I don't feel knowing the Japanese language... gives you any sort of an edge in terms of your analysis... I think it's the culture side that's more important than the language." — Directly rebuts the common "language/data access" edge thesis, including the host's own framing that AI is closing that gap. "It's very important to understand that you should not overstay your welcome... you've got to know when you got to take your money and run for the hills." — Core, actionable risk-management principle distinguishing Japan from buy-and-hold markets. "If you want to invest in SoftBank, I always say to people, the investment case is just one line: it's all about Mr. Son... Market's view of Mr. Son is a bit like a pendulum... you basically need to buy the shares when the pendulum goes towards the idiot side." — Concrete, non-fundamental sentiment-cycle trading heuristic for a top former holding.
