Margin normalization : Murphy accepts 60-70% gross margins (vs. historical 80-90% SaaS norms) as the new bar for "great" AI companies, with margin expansion path via inference optimization and proprietary/own-model data — explicitly cited for Lovable. Best Quotes "You're better off being in [outliers] at a very small percent than owning a large percent of a company that exits for $300 to $500 million." — Murphy. Signals the industry-wide abandonment of ownership-target discipline as the underwriting anchor. "I don't think it goes to that 96% because... if I use Anthropic it actually increases my customer retention, I generate more revenue, I get users to engage with the platform more." — Murphy. Core rebuttal to the open-source-commoditization bear case for frontier labs — though see Disagreements below. "This company is wildly profitable and at a scale that would probably shock most people... I feel like we're just on the cusp of it, and this company is already a beast." — Murphy, on OpenRouter. Rare non-public signal on the routing layer's economics from a board member. "There's no way in hell that we're going to have 60 independent model companies... huge concentrated positions for some firms. So I think that's a challenge." — Murphy. An insider with stakes in 7 neo-labs flagging his own category as overheated. Disagreements & Conviction Open source vs. frontier economics (host presses hard, Murphy holds a soft line) : Murphy resists the displacement thesis twice but immediately hedges into a blended multi-model future, and his own OpenRouter/Lovable commentary (cost optimization, "complementary" own-model builds) functionally validates the disintermediation dynamic he verbally downplays. Read as a real but incompletely reconciled position, not a settled conviction. Ownership doesn't matter — except when it visibly still stung : Stated with high confidence ("by far"), but when the ho

title: Lenny's Podcast — Why the people building AI can’t tell you what’s next | Dianne Penn (Anthropic)
text: Diane Penn (Anthropic) on Product, Evals, and the Exponential — Research Memo Thesis Anthropic's product edge comes from a repeatable pattern — spot an unlabeled use-case shift early (longform coding, agentic harnesses), ship a cheap model tweak paired with a genuine product vehicle, and let bottoms-up culture iterate fast — while the org's own methodology (evals over PRDs) and safety-gating practices are themselves becoming structural variables worth tracking, not just cultural color. Key Points Opus 3 (guest recalls "early March 2024," hedged) was deliberately trained to improve longform code generation, not just autocomplete — a "relatively smaller change from a training perspective" that became an outsized early competitive differentiator with developers, at a time "nobody said Anthropic and Claude and coding in the same sentence." Opus 3.5's breakout was co-dependent on Claude Code as a product vehicle: "Opus 3.5 wouldn't have had that moment without a product like Claude Code, and Claude Code wouldn't have had that type of adoption accelerated without Opus 3.5." "Golden Gate Claude" (a 24-hour, cross-functional ship off an interpretability research finding, reaching only ~2,000 users) is cited by Penn as the moment the team felt it could build differentiated experiences fast — the concrete origin story behind Anthropic's bottoms-up shipping culture. Labs (which Penn's team supports) operates on small pods, strong conviction on theme , weak conviction on exact prototype , and a willingness to kill bets and revisit "in one to two model generations" — this is the mechanism behind Claude Code, MCP, Skills, and Claude Design, not generic "innovation culture." Product methodology has shifted: "evals are the new PRDs" — user pain points are operationalized as eval sets rather than specs; PRDs persist mainly for cross-team alignment (legal, safety, engineering) and for ambiguous, not-yet-defined bets. Capability jumps are discontinuous per scaling-law research — the "loss" curve is smooth but capabilities emerge suddenly, meaning Anthropic itself doesn't always know what a model can do until evals surface it ("product overhang and user overhang"). Post-Fable/Mythos scrutiny led Anthropic to build new fallback UX/safety infrastructure (the "model safeguards package"); Penn states this is an active, evolving investment area "in the coming weeks and months." Shipping cadence: "four models for the whole year" in 2024 vs. more than that volume "in just Q2 of this year" (year of recording unspecified in transcript — do not read as "Q2 2025"). Writing quality is named as a current, deliberate investment gap ("very active efforts on my team and on the research side about making Claude write better"), framed as the next "jagged edge" after agentic capability gains. Alignment/constitution-driven pushback is framed as a capability advantage, not a limitation — used internally even for pricing decisions on the next Claude version via a research model. Best Quotes "Opus 3.5 wouldn't have had that moment without a product like Claude Code, and Claude Code wouldn't have had that type of adoption accelerated without Opus 3.5." — Diane Penn. States Anthropic's model+product co-dependency thesis directly. "We actually have a saying on the team of 'evals are the new PRDs.'" — Diane Penn. Names the structural shift in how the org defines and measures user value. "In 2024, we shipped four models for the whole year... I think we did more than that volume in just Q2 of this year." — Diane Penn. Quantified, rare acceleration data point — but note "this year" is undated in transcript. "The latest number I saw was Anthropic was making like, I don't know, $50 billion in ARR." — Host. Material figure, but explicitly hedged/secondhand by the host himself — not company guidance. Disagreements & Conviction Host vs. Penn on "unfair advantage" from restricted model access : Host argues gated frontier-model access (post-Mythos) creates a real internal-use edge for labs. Penn deflects to a stated inclusivity goal ("to not have that happen... one of our top priorities right now") without engaging the mechanism. Conviction: soft/diplomatic on Penn's side — this reads as an unresolved tension, not a rebuttal, and is worth tracking independently. Penn's stated ideal vs. practice : Penn wants frontier tech "as inclusive as possible," yet describes actively building more gating/red-teaming infrastructure because of Fable-era restrictions. Framed by her as temporary/solvable, moderate conviction. Coding as inflection point : Already-resolved consensus by the time of taping (Dario's "coding solved" call was doubted, then vindicated) — not a live non-consensus view today, useful only as a pattern (Anthropic spots unlabeled use-case shifts early). Token-maxing framing : Host endorses Gary Tan's "$100K/year tokens = living in 2028" framing; Penn mildly reframes spend as an input, not the goal — "the output is... experimentation." Low conviction disagreement, more a nuance-add than a rebuttal. Notably absent: no hard host pushback anywhere in the interview on ARR sustainability, competitive threat, or safety-cost tradeoffs — treat unchallenged claims (culture-driven speed, evals-as-PRDs, writing-gap-as-prioritization) as company narrative, not stress-tested fact. Investment Implications Model+harness bundling as moat (near-term, intensifying 12–18 mo): Favors labs that ship their own agentic harness (Anthropic/Claude Code, OpenAI/Codex, Microsoft/GitHub Copilot) over model-only entrants or thin API-wrapper startups, whose differentiation risks being absorbed once the lab ships its own product layer (Skills, Tag, Claude Design cited as in-house builds). [Model inference from stated Opus 3.5/Claude Code co-dependency.] Eval infrastructure demand (current practice at frontier labs, 1–3 yr enterprise diffusion): "Evals are the new PRDs" plausibly benefits eval/observability tooling (LangSmith, Braintrust-type vendors) as enterprises adopti

title: No Priors — Building an Autonomous Delivery Experience with DoorDash Co-Founders Andy Fang and Stanley Tang
text: DoorDash: Agentic Commerce, Robotics, and the Multimodal Fleet — Research Memo Thesis DoorDash is running two under-appreciated platform bets simultaneously — an AI-native ordering interface (Ask DoorDash) that is unlocking latent discovery/basket-size demand, and an in-house autonomy stack (DOT) built from eight years of operational data that management argues is structurally hard to replicate. The bottleneck for both has shifted from "does the model/robot work" to operations, hardware supply chain, and unproven enterprise-AI ROI — meaning execution risk, not technology risk, is now the swing factor. Key Points Ask DoorDash (conversational ordering): 50% of restaurant-search trajectories are orders from places users never ordered from before; grocery baskets run ~40% larger, driven by use cases like fridge-photo meal planning and dietary-constraint reordering. (Fang; transcript-supported) Modality history: DoorDash initially bet on voice as the interface for conversational commerce; that didn't land, and text/chat won instead — a disclosed false start worth weighting against current conviction in the CLI/agent-first roadmap. Robotics timeline: Autonomy R&D began in 2018 as a skunkworks effort (~half an engineer's time), initially via partnerships with sidewalk-robot and robotaxi players. DoorDash concluded neither category fit its 3–5 mile, ~15-minute suburban delivery profile and built DOT in-house instead. DOT specs and status: 300 lb, up to 20 mph, designed for bike lanes and roads (not sidewalk-only, not robotaxi). Live in Phoenix for almost two years; reached full L4 (fully autonomous) status last year — i.e., roughly the first year of Phoenix operation was not yet full L4 (this sequencing is stated in two separate remarks by Ting, not a single clean claim). Data moat claim: Ting argues DoorDash's historical human-Dasher drop-off location data solves the "first and last 100 feet" problem (exact pickup/dropoff points) in a way no generic mapping or autonomy dataset can — "that data doesn't exist anywhere else." Bottleneck has moved: Per Ting, autonomy itself is "increasingly becoming less and less of a constraint"; the harder problems now are operations/fleet management (depots, maintenance, battery/regen-braking edge cases, robot boot-up scripts breaking at scale) and hardware manufacturing/supply chain. DoorDash partnered with Also, a micromobility company spun out of Rivian, for vehicle-scale manufacturing (chaired by "RJ" per the transcript — surname "Scaringe" is outside knowledge, not stated in transcript). Labor forecast (non-consensus): Ting predicts more Dashers in 10 years, not fewer, arguing human supply can't scale 5–10x with GOV growth (25% YoY off 9M Dashers, 3B+ annual deliveries) and that a multimodal fleet (DOT, drones, sidewalk bots, humans) expands total addressable delivery volume rather than substituting for it. Internal AI spend/ROI: Fang states internal AI/coding tool spend rose ~20x from January to June (year not specified in transcript) and has since flatlined, attributed to intentional cost discipline (routing cheaper tasks to open-weight models) rather than reduced usage. Coding shows clear ROI; non-technical/enterprise use cases (accounting, analytics, QBR automation) show a gap between "works okay" self-reports and weaker real performance on scrubbed enterprise data versus lab demos — an open, unresolved question for DoorDash (harness/tooling gap vs. genuine model capability gap). DoorDash released "Dashbench" to quantify this. Adjacent, under-covered initiatives: DoorDash acquired a company called Metis last year to bring AI-native practices into the org (context for the spend/ROI push). It also launched "Tasks," using its Dasher fleet to collect data points for training world models — a parallel data-monetization angle alongside DOT that received no analytical attention in this memo's predecessor artifacts. Best Quotes "50% of trajectories of people using Ask DoorDash for restaurants... are people ordering from places they've never ordered from before, which is huge because that's one of the hardest metrics historically for DoorDash for us to move." — Fang. Concrete evidence AI-driven discovery expands behavior, not just convenience. "The autonomy is probably increasingly becoming less and less of a constraint of a blocker. It's really like now how do you... scale operations... And then the last piece is hardware... now it's starting to look like hardware is starting to become [the bottleneck]." — Ting. Reframes DOT's risk profile from AI risk to capex/supply-chain risk. "My prediction actually is in a world where robotics, drones, AI is everywhere... in 10 years time, we're actually going to have more Dashers doing deliveries, not less." — Ting. High-conviction, falsifiable counter to the "robots replace gig workers" bear case. "When we then send somebody's data to the labs... the models crush it. But then... when we actually have it with the enterprise data with all the real stuff, it's not performing as well." — Fang. A candid, non-promotional admission that tempers the AI-productivity narrative for anything beyond coding. Disagreements & Conviction Build vs. partner in autonomy: DoorDash spent several years believing it could be "the platform" layer atop third-party robots, then reversed to build DOT in-house. Management frames this as deliberate iterative learning; the plain sequence of events (years of partnering before pivoting) reads at least partly as a strategy that didn't pay off before the in-house pivot. Moderate conviction the "we always intended this" framing is somewhat retrospective smoothing — worth discounting management's foresight narrative on future long-term bets (e.g., Tasks/world-model data). Tech-first vs. use-case-first industry critique: Ting stakes out a contrarian view that most autonomy/robotics/AI startups build technology first and retroactively search for a use case; the host independently volunteers the same critique

title: Hidden Forces — How to Win a Trade War | Chad Bown
text: Chad Bown on Trade War — Research Memo Thesis The current era of "trade war" is really three distinct conflicts bundled together — political grievance, sector protectionism, and genuine national-security resilience concerns — and only the last is economically defensible; Bown's key structural claim is that concentration of production (not trade itself) is the real vulnerability, with China's 2020 "dual circulation" strategy the pivotal doctrine engineering one-way Western dependence (evidenced by ~90% rare-earth/magnet dominance now demonstrably weaponizable). Key Points Three drivers of US tariff policy, per Bown: (1) grievance politics, (2) industry protectionism, (3) national-security resilience — he argues only #3 justifies a trade-war response; the first two are largely non-economic. Falsifiable finding cited by Bown: recent economist studies show trade-shocked voters backed Trump's tariffs even when the tariffs left them worse off (fewer jobs, less local production) — support is grievance-driven, not outcome-driven. Weaponized interdependence is a mixed bag empirically: more bilateral trade lowers war probability between the two parties, but trade concentrated in one relationship (crowding out a third party) raises conflict odds with the excluded party — Bown's own stated caveat, illustrated via Germany's Russian gas dependence emboldening Putin pre-invasion. China's 2020 "dual circulation" speech (Xi Jinping) is Bown's named turning point: Beijing deliberately reduces its own import dependence while increasing the West's dependence on it — now backed by ~90% global share of rare earths/permanent magnets, with a stated transmission mechanism (a cutoff could nearly halt Western auto production). Iran/Strait of Hormuz shock avoided a 1970s-style oil-embargo recession — Bown attributes resilience to strategic reserves (US SPR, opaque-but-inferred Chinese reserve drawdown visible in collapsed import data) and demand-side adjustments in exposed Asian economies. Concentration ≠ trade dependence: Bown's clearest analytical move is the infant-formula example — a US shortage traced to over-reliance on a single domestic Michigan plant , resolved by importing from Switzerland — demonstrating that diversification (including via trade) mitigates risk that autarky does not. Root cause of anti-globalization backlash, per Bown (stated as his explicit bias): US failure to build redistribution/adjustment policy, not trade openness itself — contrasted with Nordic Europe's welfare-state complement to openness. Reshoring today would likely reward capital (automation) over displaced labor. No coherent single US objective exists, per Bown — unlike China's codified doctrine, US trade policy hinges on one unpredictable individual (Trump), making it structurally harder to forecast than Beijing's. The Drezner point ("wars aren't purely economic") is explicitly a secondhand citation by Bown, not his own independent analysis — relevant for attribution precision. Best Quotes "If you and I trading more together comes at the expense of me trading less with Sally, then it's actually more likely that I might go to war with Sally... because I don't need Sally." — Bown. Key mechanism for reading which excluded third parties face rising conflict risk as US/China build separate blocs. "China produces 90% of the world's supply of this stuff... China cuts off supplies... we almost have to shut down our automobile industry." — Bown. Concrete, quantified chokepoint with a stated real-economy transmission channel. "[Voters] even though his tariffs didn't make them any better off... they still voted for him anyway." — Bown. Tariff politics are sticky regardless of economic outcome — implies durability of the regime even where it fails cost-benefit tests. "Assuming that he's seeking to achieve anything that we would consider falling within the national interest; it could just be an extension of political graft and corruption." — Host. Non-consensus framing that undercuts rational-actor models of US tariff trajectory forecasting. Disagreements & Conviction Trade openness vs. redistribution failure as root cause of backlash : Bown holds this strongly and explicitly as his stated personal bias ("trade is generally good... unequivocally") — a direct, high-conviction rebuttal of the "trade hollowed out the middle of the country" narrative common in populist and much financial-media commentary. Capital-recycling/asset-inflation thesis (host-driven) : Host advances a specific structural claim (dollar reserve status → capital recycling → US asset appreciation concentrated among capital owners). Bown does not rebut but also does not validate magnitude: "I don't have an exact number," then pivots back to his standard redistribution prescription. This is an unresolved line of inquiry, not a real clash — treat as open, not settled. Weaponized interdependence validity : Bown treats Russia-Ukraine and Iran/Hormuz as genuinely mixed evidence, explicitly warning "we don't want to push [the evidence] too far" since it's drawn from non-experimental history. Moderate conviction — a real epistemic caveat, not hedging for politeness. "Politics first, economics second" framing : This is the host's closing monologue, delivered with no recorded verbal response from Bown (not "tacit agreement" — simply no engagement before the segment cut to the paywall). Investment Implications Rare-earth/magnet supply chain (1st order, transcript-supported mechanism) : Western automakers, defense primes, and electronics OEMs face input risk from China's ~90% share; alternative producers (e.g., MP Materials, Lynas) benefit from policy-driven demand. 2026–2030 horizon. Subsidy-dependent capacity buildout (2nd order, MODEL INFERENCE) : Because concentration — not trade — is the actual vulnerability, Western rare-earth capacity built to address it may be structurally uneconomic without permanent subsidy, risking boom-bust dynamics on policy headlines rather than fundam

title: Odd Lots — Branko Milanovic on What Comes After Globalization | Odd Lots
text: The Great Global Transformation: Milanović on National Market Liberalism — Research Memo Thesis Milanović argues the neoliberal globalization order (1989–2016) is being replaced by "national market liberalism" — domestically neoliberal, internationally mercantilist, zero-/negative-sum — a shift he dates to Trump 2016 and describes as continued (not reversed) by Biden. The most durable investment implication is that this regime is politically self-sustaining: because the redistribution valve at home stays closed, the political energy from the Western middle-class squeeze channels permanently into trade/industrial policy rather than fiscal policy, making tariffs/reshoring a multi-cycle, bipartisan theme rather than a Trump-specific trade. Key Points Periodization : Milanović frames post-1974 history as four economic orders, culminating in "national market liberalism" — domestic free-pricing/competition/low redistribution retained, but the international leg (free trade, capital/goods mobility) "chopped off" in favor of mercantilism. Elephant chart restated : Western middle-class per-capita growth ~1%/yr vs. ~3%+ for the Western top and for China (his framing, not a rigorous fresh calculation) — his explanation for why governments chose to blame trade/China rather than pursue redistribution or reskilling (a political choice, he argues, not an economic necessity). China consumption/savings : consumption-to-GDP ~40-45% vs. US 70%, India 50%; he floats that wage compression and retained SOE profits may be a deliberate political-economy choice funding rail, AI, EVs, space, and (nascent) aircraft manufacturing — but he explicitly caveats "I'm not a macroeconomist" and "I'm not quite sure if they really... cannot [rebalance]." Treat as informed speculation, not his core research finding. China elite income shift : in Chinese urban top-5% data, share of elite income from SOE/government/Party jobs went from ~two-thirds (1988) to ~one-third (2018/2023), reversing to two-thirds private-sector — a shift he says took ~40 years vs. ~150 years in England's capitalist-class formation (per Bob Allen's data, though Milanović's own English date range — "1688 and I suppose 1900" — is a hedged recollection, not a precise cited figure). Global inequality pivot : China's growth has flipped from inequality-reducing to inequality-increasing at the world level (it's now rich enough that further growth widens the gap to poor countries); he argues the 21st century's inequality trajectory now hinges on India and 5-6 large African economies (~1bn people, the only population still growing ~2%/yr). Homoploutia : his coined term for a US top-10% cohort simultaneously top-decile in both labor and capital income — he calls it a likely new phenomenon but self-hedges: "I would venture to say," and notes researchers are actively checking whether it existed in the 1920s-30s. Treat novelty as provisional, not established. Trump/Xi/Putin "anti-money-elite" framing : Milanović's book line drew direct host pushback (Trump's admin is tax-cut-orthodox and business-heavy). He conceded substantially — retreating to "the voters who elected Trump were reacting against neoliberalism's winners," not that Trump's policies redistribute from capital to labor. The stronger version of his claim applies to Xi (Jack Ma IPO cancellation, delivered via a "mid-level official," as deliberate signaling) and Putin, not Trump. Efficiency vs. security fault line : Milanović initially dismissed complaints about Chinese manufacturing dominance ("let them be producing X, Y, Z... why do we complain?") but partially conceded the Hamiltonian dual-use/sovereignty argument once pressed by the host — an unresolved seam in his own framework (his book's ch. 2 cites both Montesquieu's trade-brings-peace view and Hobson/Lenin/Luxemburg's trade-brings-conflict view without picking one). Europe's bind : needs cheap energy but cut off Russian gas for costlier US energy; needs immigration to offset demographic decline but is broadly closing the door (Spain the outlier, for Latin American immigration specifically). He frames European alignment with Trump's China hawkishness as defensive/situational ("tiger in a cage... please the tiger"), not strategic conviction — Germany specifically driven by EV competition. Policy preference : he favors a "pedagogical tax" on extraordinary wealth (aligned with Zucman/Piketty) — explicitly non-committal on rate ("I don't really have a view whether it should be 2%, 20%") but firm that the political purpose (signaling wealth doesn't buy governance) matters more than the number. Best Quotes "China's consumption-to-GDP ratio is very low, it's like about 40-45%. US is 70%... I think there is a political-economy reason why China needs to have... these large amounts of money" — Milanović. Non-consensus challenge to the "China consumption rebalancing" thesis — but delivered immediately after "I'm not a macroeconomist," so weight accordingly. "In 1988... two-thirds of the income of the elite comes from state-owned enterprises... go today... it's the reverse... China is just at the level that we have not historically seen" — Milanović. His strongest, most concretely-sourced empirical claim; bears directly on how durable private Chinese wealth accumulation is. "If China is efficient and too good and producing X, Y, and Z, let them be producing X, Y, and Z. Why do we complain about this?" — Milanović. Reveals the live, unresolved tension between efficiency logic and security logic that underlies the entire tariff/reshoring debate — even a sympathetic economist doesn't fully resolve it. "When Jack Ma was told that he's not going to have his IPO, the phone call was made by a mid-level official... things don't happen by accident in China. That was a message." — Milanović. Concrete mechanism for how to read future regulatory strikes on Chinese private capital/tech founders. Disagreements & Conviction Efficiency vs. sovereignty (China manufacturing domi

title: Excess Returns — He Called It the Worst Chart Imaginable. Then He Bought It | Rupert Mitchell on Cracks in the Mag 7
text: Blind Squirrel Macro: Equity Issuance, China's Oil Collar, and the Global Value Hunt — Research Memo Thesis Rupert Mitchell's core structural call — that AI-capex-driven equity issuance (SpaceX's ~$86B IPO, Google's $85B raise) is reversing the buyback-driven de-equitization tailwind that has propped up US mega-cap equities for 15 years — is live and working via his long RSP/short QQQ pair trade (+10% since late June). But the flagship top-down expression of his broader underweight-US thesis, the "Chart of Truth" (S&P vs. rest-of-world), has gone flat/dead since November despite a stronger dollar, so the intra-US rotation trade is currently outperforming the global rotation trade it's meant to validate. Key Points Equity issuance / de-equitization reversal : Google's $85B capital raise ("a real wake-up call") and SpaceX's IPO signal AI capex is now funded via new shares, not buybacks/debt — removing a structural equity-demand tailwind. Live trade: long RSP, short QQQ, +10% since third week of June, held in Bushy's hedgebook, 12–24 month horizon. Grounded partly in Meb Faber's study on dropping the largest S&P stock annually. Chart of Truth (S&P vs. rest-of-world) — flat since November , despite the dollar being "punchy" (DXY >100), which would typically hurt rest-of-world equities but hasn't. Momentum trades are "rolling over right now quite painfully." This is the report card on his broader underweight-US call, and it's stalled even as the narrower RSP/QQQ trade works — an important distinction the transcript keeps separate but easy to conflate. Oil/China "collar" : China's monopsony buying behavior has effectively written a put near high-$60s/barrel while capping upside — Mitchell expects spikes into triple digits but not sustained triple-digit prices. This underwrites energy-equity capex (E&Ps, integrators, midstream, offshore services, Canadian E&Ps) without requiring a bullish oil price call. Trimmed refiners this week ("felt like sacrilege"). Separately, his own directional crude position has round-tripped and had "a very punishing week" — the crude trade and energy-equity thesis are explicitly decoupled ("No triple digits. It's not based on that"). Gold/precious metals : ~30-40% underweight his target sizing (down from 9-10% late last year); expects further near-term pain if the Fed delivers an unpriced hike, plans to rebuild after. Framed as a portfolio diversifier/bond substitute, not a permabull inflation call. Bonds : Structurally underweight/dislikes duration because stock-bond correlation has flipped positive; currently "red-teaming" this bias mid-conversation but resolving toward T-bill cash (optionality) over duration exposure, even while acknowledging a Fed cutting cycle may be imminent. Fed event (next-day, binary) : Market pricing ~31.5% odds (down from 34%) of a hike. Mitchell doesn't expect a 50bp "death shot" — cites financing constraints on the government/data-center capex/private credit complex — but flags historical base rate risk (no unpriced hike since Greenspan's Nov 1994 surprise 75bp, under a new, guidance-averse Fed chair). A 25bp hike is a non-event; a 50bp surprise would hit risk assets hard, especially momentum tech. UK small/mid-caps : Bullish via investment trusts (high-single-digit NAV discounts), citing 5 FTSE 100 take-privates this year, 40% net cash + buybacks across the FTSE 250, and possible state-driven pension capital repatriation ("mandation") — the latter explicitly flagged by Mitchell himself as speculative/hopeful, not a firm call. Political "peak populism" read (Farage vs. Count Binface) is tentative; the M&A/buyback support is firmer. Uzbekistan : Long GDRs in the Templeton-managed Uzbekistan National Privatization Fund (London-listed, IPO'd May, +30% since, still low-single-digit earnings multiples). Governance backstop from Templeton's prior Romania privatization playbook. Sizing commentary in transcript is garbled/ambiguous ("a small single-digit allocation could be 20% of a portfolio down the line") — treat as directional color, not a precise target. Turkey : Long top-20 index names near 10x forward earnings, despite historical inflation volatility (CPI ~80% in '22); thesis rests on dollar-resilient equity performance, low US-consumer reliance (2%), defense exports, and logistics/energy-hub positioning, not on inflation normalization. Portfolio (Bushy) positioning/risk : Re-risked from 35-40% cash/hedges (Mar/Apr) back into energy equities, crude, wheat/cotton, and the RSP/QQQ pair. Has outperformed the S&P since start of last year on <50% of its volatility. Despite the re-risking, Mitchell is tactically cautious short-term — adding VIX hedges on record-low implied equity correlation and elevated leverage, warning of a possible rerun of "the leverage unwind... two summers ago." This barbell (long core conviction + long vol hedge) is a stance, not a contradiction, but PMs replicating exposure should note the hedge is tactical, not a signal to de-risk the core book. Best Quotes "If you think of the lynchpin of US equities over the last 10 to 15 years—take away the buybacks, take away 401(k) flows... a massive tailwind has turned into a huge headwind." — Rupert Mitchell. Core causal mechanism for the structural US-equity thesis. "China has effectively become a monopsony... China has written a put on... high 60s a barrel... I think we could see energy prices spike into triple digits, but I really don't think that they stay there for very long." — Rupert Mitchell. Non-consensus mechanism reframing energy-equity risk/reward without a bullish oil price call. "We were close to the 200-day moving average... And now we're dead. We're just dead... we're back to flat... notwithstanding the fact that the dollar has actually felt a little bit punchy." — Rupert Mitchell. title: Founders — How Obsession Built Christopher Nolan
text: Christopher Nolan on Obsession, Constraints, and Control — Research Memo Source: Tom Shone's The Nolan Variations , discussed via podcast summary. Shone conducted years of exclusive direct interviews with Nolan — a firsthand primary source. Thesis Nolan converts operating discipline (speed, cost control, secrecy, analog-format commitment) directly into negotiating leverage over studios, and this — not raw talent alone — explains how a director with no consistent budget history (from near-zero on Following to $200M+ tentpoles) reached "unassailable" creative autonomy after The Dark Knight . The durable, testable divergence is his refusal to adopt industry-standard digital workflows since 2006, sustained for 20 years as a deliberate differentiation/control strategy rather than nostalgia. Key Points Nolan has written or co-written all 11 of his films; his films have earned $5B+ box office, giving him rare standing to greenlight original scripts at scale — but his budgets have ranged from micro-budget ( Following , weekend shoots funded by his own cameraman-job bonus) to $40M (a film he calls a deliberately tight budget) to $200M+ tentpoles. Correction from QA: the claim that "all 11 films" carried $200M+ budgets is false and was struck. Explicit stated mechanism: cost/speed discipline buys creative control. "If I can work a little bit faster... a little bit cheaper than people expect, then they'll let me do my thing." Post- Dark Knight ($1B+ box office), his position at Warner Bros. went from "solid to unassailable," directly unlocking greenlight for Inception — an idea he'd carried since age 16 (~23-year gestation, per Nolan's own later, more precise figure; he initially misspoke and revised "10 years" to "20" before landing on 23). Since The Prestige (2006), Nolan has never adopted the industry-standard digital-negative/digital-edit workflow — still shoots film, edits electronically, then hand-cuts the negative from frame numbers. A 20-year, self-described act of separating from industry consensus. Nolan is a self-described pessimist who "always plan[s] for the worst," a contrast with reality-distortion-field-style founder confidence; he pairs this with insisting he must believe each film is "the best film that's ever been made" — a barbell of maximal conviction + maximal downside planning (inference on the synthesis, not a claim Nolan makes explicitly). He rejects the "90% of information is online" assumption, estimating the true figure near 0.9%; Shone's own informal test (10 facts pulled from library books) found only 1 of 10 online — directionally corroborating, but an n=10, single-sample anecdote, not a validated statistic. Production culture mirrors the same control logic: only 20 of 600+ Dunkirk crew read the script; copies were watermarked to trace leaks; he refuses a second unit and shoots every frame himself; he resists large outsourced VFX/concept-art "beasts" ("I need a robot... figure me out a robot... which didn't suit my way of working at all"). Cult-level fan intensity is transcript-attested, not inferred: "Critics have received death threats when they give his films a bad review," and Nolan reciprocally normalizes fan obsession over Memento/Inception as something he shares rather than finds strange. Best Quotes "I can get my power from spending less and moving faster... If I can work a little bit faster than people expect, if I can work a little bit cheaper than people expect, then they'll let me do my thing." — Nolan. The explicit causal chain from operating discipline to creative leverage. "I am very much a pessimist. I always plan for the worst." — Nolan (verbatim; earlier draft misquoted as "I'm"). Risk posture underlying his execution reliability. "Our feeling is that 90% of the information is online. I have a suspicion that the real answer is 0.9%." — Nolan. A specific, falsifiable, non-consensus claim about digital-knowledge coverage. "The Prestige was very much the point at which we separated from the rest of the industry, or rather they separated from us." — Nolan. Dated origin of a 20-year-sustained contrarian production choice. Disagreements & Conviction Nolan vs. industry consensus on workflow/control (highest conviction, transcript-explicit): rejects standard digital pipeline, standard VFX-farm staffing, chronological storytelling convention, war-film genre convention (Dunkirk). Stated as structural and career-long, not situational — this is the one genuinely load-bearing non-consensus stance in the material. Pessimism vs. "best film ever" conviction : both stated repeatedly and with high conviction but never reconciled by Nolan or Shone in the transcript. Reading them as a coherent "barbell" posture is a reasonable but unstated inference — flag it as such downstream. "It's the person not the tools" vs. Nolan's own tool-specificity : the host's editorializing (built around Cormac McCarthy's typewriter) is only loosely extended to Nolan; it should not be read as Nolan's own claim. Nolan's actual position is closer to the opposite — his choice of film-over-digital is treated as materially, not incidentally, important. 0.9% information claim vs. tech-sector "everything is searchable" consensus : worth taking seriously directionally, but the corroborating "test" is a single 10-item sample — do not treat "0.9%" as a validated figure. Investment Implications IMAX / film-stock / specialty post supply chain (medium confidence, multi-year horizon): Nolan's bankability keeps an analog production pipeline commercially viable (film stock, hand-cutting, 70mm/IMAX finishing) purely to service his preference, plausibly extending to other directors imitating "prestige-via-analog" positioning. First-order: transcript-supported behavior. Second-order (durability of the trend beyond Nolan, market share effects): inference. title: Chit Chat Stocks — David Tepper: The Bounce Back King (Hedge Fund Legend)
text: David Tepper (Appaloosa Management) — Research Memo Thesis Tepper's edge is capital-structure and asset-class flexibility, not a single repeatable formula: across four decades he has generated some of the industry's best long-run returns (estimated 36% gross/28.5% net annualized, 1993–2013) by buying whatever is most mispriced in a crisis — sovereign debt, fraud-era corporate bonds, bank equity/debt — wherever a hard-asset floor or government backstop created asymmetric recovery value. That specific edge (distressed/crisis positioning with capital-structure access) is largely invisible in his current 13F, which now looks like a fairly consensus AI/semiconductor/megacap book. Key Points Track record (unofficial estimate): 1993–2013 Appaloosa reportedly compounded 36% gross / 28.5% net annually ($1M → $181M) — hosts rank this behind only Renaissance, and on par with/better than Druckenmiller and Soros. Not confirmed by Tepper; no public letters or audited returns exist. "Bounce-back king" pattern: Large drawdowns followed by outsized recoveries — Appaloosa reportedly fell 29% in 1998 on the Russian default, then posted 61% in 1999; fell 27% in 2008, then 132% in 2009. Pattern: he doubled down into crises rather than exiting, betting on recovery value. Russia (1998–99): Bought Russian sovereign debt (domestic and USD-denominated) as low as 5 cents on the dollar, betting a nuclear superpower's physical/economic capacity implied recovery value above zero, even after Russia's actual default. Restructured payouts plus a commodity-price rebound drove the recovery. Enron/WorldCom (2001–02): Bought ~$1B of Enron bonds at pennies on the dollar against pipeline-asset recovery value plus a $15B fraud settlement won from complicit banks; repeated the playbook with WorldCom's fiber assets. Thesis: fraud can zero the equity but not necessarily the hard assets. GFC/"Tepper bottom" (2008–09): Bought BofA common as low as $3/share against the Treasury's own stated $6 conversion price in its 2009 capital-assistance white paper; bought Citigroup bonds at 19¢, AIG debt at 10¢; bought Wachovia/WaMu preferreds ahead of forced mergers. Reportedly Appaloosa's traders were "the only major institution buying bank equity and debt" in March 2009. Result: Appaloosa +132% in 2009 (fund profit and Tepper's personal take reported as very large dollar figures, exact units ambiguous in source). Counterpoint the narrative omits: Tepper was also forced out of a well-timed short (Nasdaq bubble, 2000) by investor pressure after only a few months of losses — a limiting case showing even he wasn't immune to client-driven capitulation on a working position. Recent trades (thematic, not conviction holds): Bought Nvidia in 2023 to ride the AI theme, trimmed heavily through 2025. Bought Chinese tech (Alibaba, "anything China-related") in late 2024 on single-digit PEs plus Beijing stimulus; Alibaba roughly doubled within a year; he has since sold much of the position — framed by hosts as a trade, not a long-term thesis. Fund lifecycle: Grew to ~$20B AUM; converted to a family office in 2019 with outside capital returned — current 13F reflects only Tepper's own money. Current 13F (unverified durability given rapid turnover): Top holdings — Amazon, Micron, Google, Uber, Vistra, Nvidia, NRG, Meta, SanDisk, Corning, Taiwan Semiconductor. Heavy AI/semiconductor/power exposure. Hosts speculate (their own view, not Tepper's stated plan) that Micron and SanDisk may be exited by the next filing. Best Quotes "We're value oriented and performance based like a lot of funds, but... we're not afraid of the downside of different situations when we've done the analysis. Some other people are very afraid of losing money, which keeps them from making money." — Host, reading a direct Tepper quote. His own articulation of the mechanism behind every case study in this memo. "Tepper appears to be using multiple mental models when he invests... You would have a difficult time deciding what benchmark or comparable fund to judge him against." — Host, reading a capital-allocator blog post. Explains why style-box/13F pattern-matching fails for him specifically. "In March 2009, Appaloosa's traders reported back to Tepper that they were the only major institution buying bank equity and debt." — Host, citing a source. Concrete positioning evidence at the actual bottom — his edge came from being alone on the trade, not from consensus contrarianism. "Druckenmiller is famous for saying the only thing that really matters is the next 18 months." — Guest. The exit discipline underlying both Tepper's Nvidia trim and the broader thematic-investing playbook discussed. Disagreements & Conviction China trade validity: Host explicitly disagrees with Tepper's underlying macro read — "I think it's much more of like them pushing on a string for stimulus... I was someone that was wrong on that specific one." Guest doesn't defend the macro thesis, framing it as belief in the trade rather than the businesses. Conviction: candid, low-stakes admission, not a hedge — a useful discipline (separating "the trade worked" from "the thesis was right"). "Don't fight the Fed" is now consensus, not contrarian: Guest notes today's assumption of a Fed/government backstop is retroactive — in 2008–09 "that was not the thinking... it probably seemed like the Fed didn't have control." Stated plainly as historical fact-check. Implication: the 2009-style edge (disbelieving in a backstop others doubted) has likely compressed as the playbook became public knowledge. Applicability of Tepper's style to individual investors: Guest oscillates — first disclaims relevance ("not managing my portfolio as actively... not sure there's a ton to take away"), then articulates a specific transferable lesson (keep dry powder to rotate into crisis-driven distress). Read as genuine uncertainty, not false modesty; the dry-powder lesson is the one takeaway that survives his own skepticism. Investment Implications 13F-fol

title: We Study Billionaires — How to Find Hidden Investment Treasures w/ Christopher Begg (RWH070)
text: East Coast Asset Management — Chris Begg on Graphs, Clouds, and Value 3.0 — Research Memo Thesis East Coast Asset Management (Chris Begg) runs a sub-10-holding, 16-year concentrated portfolio underwritten to 15%+ 10-year IRRs, built on a repeatable pattern: identify durable "graph" businesses (increasing returns to scale as nodes/edges densify) and buy them when a market "cloud" (perceived-but-unproven risk) diverges from underlying evidence. The current live expressions of this — Google (thesis largely realized), Constellation Software (new, contrarian), and Tesla/SpaceX (largest, most aggressive, most idiosyncratic) — are the actionable, trackable positions; the surrounding philosophy (writing, attention, trust) is culture/process context, not itself investable signal. Key Points Framework : Three-pillar quality screen (widening moat, secular tailwinds, trustworthy/capable operators) plus a 10-year DCF-style valuation targeting 15%+ IRR on free cash flow growth. Portfolio: fewer than 10 holdings, each treated as a "hypothesis" continuously retested, not a settled conclusion. Google : Begg states — without citing external data — that search volume rose alongside AI adoption (not fell to LLMs) and that the FTC antitrust overhang resolved favorably; he says they held Google at ~15x earnings before the re-rating and it remains a top holding. This is a completed, not prospective , trade — the mispricing window is described as already closed; new buyers today are paying for resolved risk, not residual asymmetry. Constellation Software : New 2025 buy after 10+ years of study, entered ~50% off highs. Uses an 8-layer "IMMORTAL" moat framework (interface/motion/memory/orchestration/resilience/trust/allocation/learning) to argue vertical system-of-record software is AI-resistant, possibly AI-additive. Explicitly framed as live/unproven: "the hypothesis is holding... we'll see." Falsification trigger he names himself: accelerating customer churn. Tesla (initiated 2025, researched since fall 2023) : Framed as five businesses — EV, FSD/robotaxi, Energy storage, Optimus robot, and an anticipated SpaceX combination. Claims FSD "solved autonomy" at ~10x human safety and cites guest/expert estimates of 80%+ of global miles autonomous within 10 years. He self-flags the estimate uncertainty as unusually wide ("our internal models are almost comical... I've never seen a range this wide") even while stating high conviction in the midpoint. SpaceX : Anticipates a Tesla/SpaceX merger "within the next 12 months" (unconfirmed, his own speculation). Cites launch cost collapsing from ~$2,400/kg to $10–100/kg via Starship, enabling Starlink direct-to-cell and orbital data centers claimed ~75% cheaper than terrestrial. Notably, he also references SpaceX being "in the public markets now" and pre-IPO compute sales to Anthropic/Google — in tension with the private-company "backdoor via EchoStar" framing used elsewhere in the conversation; scope of "public" is unclear from the transcript and should not be taken as fully resolved. Combined Tesla+SpaceX : Underwritten at ~26% IRR / 10x-in-10-years against a stated $3.2T combined valuation for "10 businesses." "Value 3.0" : Positioned as a lineage extension (Graham 1.0 → Buffett/Munger 2.0 → Sleep/Begg 3.0), requiring normalized/adjusted earnings to see true cheapness in growth investment-heavy compounders (Amazon, Google, Meta, Tesla). Used to justify Tesla-style bets as disciplined value investing rather than momentum/narrative investing — a framing worth pressure-testing rather than accepting at face value. Process discipline : Deliberately small (3-person) investment team to preserve direct contact with primary source material; explicit rejection of LLM/analyst-mediated reading of source documents, framed as protecting "judgment" (the "keystone" of the process) — notably alongside heavy personal use of AI for creative work (songwriting), a distinction he doesn't fully reconcile. Best Quotes "We are underwriting 15% or better IRRs over 10 years. And over a 16-year time period, we've been able to translate that objective into returns." — Begg. The explicit, falsifiable performance hurdle against which every position should be judged. "If you look at the combined entity of Tesla and SpaceX, you're paying $3.2 trillion for a collection of 10 businesses... I think penciling out a 26% IRR in this investment is not hard to do, to 10x over 10 years." — Begg. The single most quantified, aggressive forward-return claim in the transcript; directly testable over time. "Our internal models are almost comical because you're like, 'What? I've never seen a range this wide.'" — Begg. A rare, credibility-enhancing admission of genuine outcome uncertainty embedded inside a high-conviction position. "The minute you give an LLM or an agent... to read that source material and interpret it, I think you lose that connection with something that's really valuable." — Begg. Explains the firm's structural choice to stay small — relevant to how the process scales (or doesn't). Disagreements & Conviction Tesla investability : Begg himself previously held the consensus "uninvestable" view and reversed it after ~2 years of research and peer pushback. Conviction is high and specific (quantified IRR, safety multiple, mile-share forecast), but he simultaneously admits the outcome range is unusually wide — high conviction in the midpoint, not the precision. Software apocalypse vs. Constellation's moat : Genuinely live and provisional ("we'll see," explicit churn-based falsification criterion) — a hedged contrarian call, not dogma. Value-investing legitimacy of Tesla/SpaceX : Begg frames "value 3.0" as an unbroken extension of Graham-style asymmetry logic; skeptics (voiced by the host, not independently by a third party in this transcript) see narrative/momentum investing in value clothing. No adversarial pushback actually occurs in this conversation — the host is a friend and LP, so treat all "tension"

title: Yet Another Value — July 2026 Random Ramblings
text: Yet Another Value Podcast — July 2026 Random Ramblings — Research Memo Thesis Host Andrew Walker (solo monologue, no guest) uses this episode for self-audit rather than a stock pitch: his biggest performance drag isn't bad picks but process discipline — selling net-cash special situations too early (Nebius, Cure) and avoiding AI exposure on style-fit grounds — while his London/FTSE takeout thesis, though directionally correct on the private/public value gap, is explicitly unresolved as to why it doesn't translate into public re-rating. Key Points 3-year rule (heuristic, not settled): if a position is flat for 3 years, "the answer's probably you," not the market — but he immediately undercuts this with the 1999 value-investor-capitulation counterexample and never resolves the tension. Missed AI trade: identified AI's workflow impact in late 2025, didn't trade it — attributes this to viewing AI as "outside his wheelhouse" and over-indexing on cheap/simple setups (spin-offs at low cash-flow multiples) over recognizing an inflection. Cites a specific anecdote: Apple reportedly accepted a 100% Micron price increase without pushback ("very un-Apple-like") as a signal he could have caught. Sold winners too early: Nebius (ex-Yandex) bought ~$18-19, sold high-$20s ~15 months ago; now $230. He explicitly notes he knew "very smart people" who thought sum-of-parts was much higher than his valuation and were "proven right" — this is a sharper admission than generic impatience: he had access to the correct counter-thesis and rejected it. Cure (net-cash biotech): bought under net cash, sold near cash; stock later peaked ~$60 (Huntington's trial data), now ~$40. Nvidia/benchmark mechanics: Nvidia = 7.5% of S&P 500, so any manager benchmarked to the S&P without Nvidia exposure is mechanically "short" it — he draws a parallel to value investors' 2000-2004 outperformance as internet-heavy indexes collapsed. Stated as a clean mechanical observation, not a trade call. London/FTSE takeouts: Mitie is the 11th £1bn+ FTSE takeover YTD; EasyJet also cited as taken out at a big premium by "Apollo, I believe" (host explicitly hedges, doesn't recall the premium). Only ~11/250 (~4-5%) of FTSE 250 names get taken out in a year, so a concentrated (~10-stock) manager is likely to hold none of them and underperform despite being directionally right on value. Unresolved London puzzle: he expects takeout scarcity to mechanically boost remaining-company multiples (analogy to Australian pension inflows, S&P 500 index-buying) but states plainly it isn't happening — "I have no clue what the solution is." This is a flagged open question, not a forecast. Fundsmith reference: cites the letter's shift toward momentum/algo-responsiveness after value underperformance as a cautionary tale, agreeing it was criticized "rightly so" — this is consensus opinion-taking, not a contrarian call. Best Quotes "If you invest in a company and it's been 3 years and the stock has kind of gone nowhere... the answer's probably you." — host; his stated (but self-doubted) thesis-abandonment heuristic. "Nvidia is 7.5% of the S&P 500... if you don't own Nvidia and you're getting benchmarked to the S&P 500, you're technically short Nvidia." — host; reframes index concentration as an implicit short, relevant to any active manager avoiding AI mega-caps. "I know a lot of very smart people who thought the sum of the parts [of Nebius] was much, much higher... they've been kind of proven right." — host; his most damaging self-admission — he had the correct counter-thesis available and didn't act on it. "Every investor wants to be invested in an inefficient market until they're actually invested in an inefficient market... welcome to the party, pal." — host (paraphrasing a friend); crystallizes the emotional cost of the London value trap. Disagreements & Conviction Non-consensus/self-critical (moderate-high conviction, unresolved): He questions whether his rigid value/spin-off framework caused him to miss AI — genuinely uncertain, repeated hedging ("I don't know," "maybe I'm not counterfactually hard enough"). Consensus, not contrarian: Fundsmith criticism — he explicitly notes this is the prevailing view ("dumped on... in a lot of places"), and agrees with it. Not a differentiated take. Internally inconsistent, unresolved: He penalizes Fundsmith for chasing recent performance/momentum, then asks whether he himself should have chased AI (recent-performance-chasing) — he half-notices the double standard but doesn't reconcile it. Flagged anomaly, no resolution offered: London scarcity should (in theory) support a re-rating of remaining public names; empirically it doesn't. He states this outright as unsolved, not as a bearish or bullish call. Investment Implications AI/benchmark exposure (medium confidence, near-term/ongoing): Value/quality managers avoiding AI mega-caps are structurally short a large, ~7.5%+ swath of the benchmark; the mechanical point is transcript-stated fact. Any inference about capitulation timing (e.g., style drift clustering near tops, à la Fundsmith/1999-2000) is host-adjacent pattern-matching he gestures at but does not assert as a forecast — treat as MODEL INFERENCE. Memory/semis inflection signal (medium confidence, structural): The Micron/Apple pricing anecdote is a specific, transcript-sourced channel-check-style signal of DRAM/NAND tightness that preceded the sector rally — useful as a case study in why cash-flow-multiple screens miss inflection names, not as an active tip (this is retrospective in the transcript). UK/FTSE takeout basket (medium-high confidence on data, inference on trade construction): 11 FTSE 250 £1bn+ takeouts YTD (Mitie confirmed; EasyJet/Apollo explicitly hedged by the host — do not treat as confirmed detail) support a private->public value-gap thesis, but concentrated single-name UK value investing has a low (~4-5%/yr) hit rate on the takeout catalyst.
