title: We Study Billionaires — Meta, Adobe, & Booking Holdings | Stock Analysis & Valuation (TIP825)
text: The Investors Podcast: Meta, Booking.com, Adobe, Dolan Brands — Research Memo Thesis AI model commoditization — not model quality — is becoming the decisive competitive variable, making distribution and proprietary behavioral data the durable moats worth owning. Meta is the clearest expression of this thesis: a world-class ad machine with the strongest distribution asset in the market, trading at a discount driven by CapEx fear that may be more than priced in. The same AI-disruption sentiment has indiscriminately de-rated small/mid-cap value to levels Carlisle characterizes as historically attractive. Key Points Meta (Harry Rama, bull) - Forecasted 2026 ad revenue of $243B — $3B ahead of Google — would make Meta the #1 ad revenue generator globally; structural inflection, not yet consensus. - 2025 financials: $46B FCF, 41% operating margin, 30% net margin, 18.5% revenue CAGR over five years. - Stock down ~20% from peak at time of recording. TIP's own DCF model yields a $775 valuation vs. ~$600 spot — corroborates Harry's base-case 46% upside, which assumes no multiple re-rating, only FCF margin recovery and stable growth. - Key caveat: The 46% base case explicitly excludes subscription and cloud diversification: "They are still on the drawing board" — Harry does not model them. Optionality beyond the base case is real but unquantified. - $135B CapEx into AI infrastructure is the primary overhang. Harry's thesis: model commoditization means Meta doesn't need to win the model race — only the distribution race, which it already has. AI improves existing ad targeting economics without requiring a new revenue model. - AI caveat Harry states explicitly: "Their first LLM, Llama, was not a big success." Harry's AI confidence rests specifically on the superintelligence group's newer model, which he says has performed well against other foundational models. The bull case depends on the new model, not Llama. - If compute commoditizes, proprietary first-party social graph data (inaccessible to web crawlers like OpenAI) becomes the scarce input — Meta's walled garden is a structural data-cost advantage. Booking.com (Tobias Carlisle, cautious bull) - Operates across 220 countries via Booking.com, Priceline, Agoda, Kayak, and OpenTable. Capital-light model, does not own underlying assets. - AI disintermediation fear has driven a 6-month selloff to what Carlisle calls a "reasonable discount." He characterizes this as a contrarian AI-fear trade, not a strong conviction call. - Bull case: LLMs must access Booking's "specialized relationships" via API — Booking becomes an infrastructure layer rather than a disintermediation casualty. Historical precedent: Google attempted this disruption across Booking's entire history and failed. - Bear case (Harry, partially conceded by Tobias): Headless-API survival still means loss of discovery surface — cross-sell, on-site advertising, and browsing behavior data that currently amplify economics beyond transaction fees. Stig is the most skeptical: LLMs that know user preferences may bypass any intermediary entirely. Adobe (Stig Brodersen, bull) - ~$100B market cap, 7-year price low. 96% subscription revenue, 41M paying users. IPO'd 1986, industry standard across creative workflows. - Bull thesis: switching costs are organizational and behavioral, not merely technical. Professional identity ("inertia") and trained-workforce entrenchment make displacement slow even where AI tools are technically capable. - Product is economically cheap relative to value delivered for enterprise buyers — not where organizations cut. - Tobias's counter: Canva + ChatGPT is "vastly better than it was even a year ago. It doesn't need to be perfect." Adobe may retain a precision-dependent professional niche, but market share at the bottom erodes. He labels it "an unknowable problem." Dolan Brands (Tobias Carlisle, contrarian hold) - Stock collapsed from $27 to ~$8. Transferred from ZIG to DEEP ETF due to market cap constraints (ZIG minimum exceeded). Position trimmed from 3% to 1%, but shares were added on the decline. - Valuation: current P/S 0.4x vs. 5-year average 1.6x; current P/E 6.5x vs. historical 30x. - Business has grown slightly over the last 12 months despite headwinds. Target market: health-conscious consumers seeking protein-forward products. Bear thesis: seed oil controversy and deceleration of growth. - Tobias explicitly: "The risk of the collapse of a stock price is not reflected in the financial statements. But it does give me pause." Honest acknowledgment of value-trap risk. Macro signal (Tobias) - AI and GLP-1 disruption fears have indiscriminately de-rated small/mid-cap names regardless of magnitude of fundamental deterioration. - Carlisle states forward returns in this segment look "about as good as they have since I've been running the funds" — his strongest macro signal in the episode. Best Quotes 1. "Models are pretty much getting commoditized. That means the incremental difference between models is getting saturated. Distribution becomes more advantageous; it's the distribution that matters." — Harry Rama Significance: The load-bearing mechanism of Meta's AI bull case — reframes the CapEx risk by arguing Meta doesn't need to win the model race. 2. "The problem with spending on this type of stuff is that the chips age faster than infrastructure has in the past. It's not like a railway or fiber optic cable, which sits in the ground for a really long period of time." — Tobias Carlisle Significance: Directly challenges the durability of $135B Meta CapEx — short GPU useful lives mean reinvestment is structural, not one-time, and FCF normalization may be delayed indefinitely. 3. "Data becomes the key commodity and the scarce commodity. That's where companies like Facebook, who have a walled garden, have an advantage. title: Yet Another Value — June 2026 Random Ramblings
text: Yet Another Value Podcast — June 2026 Monthly Ramblings — Research Memo Thesis AI proliferation is creating a bifurcated value landscape: trusted credentialed brands become scarcer and more valuable as AI slop floods the information environment, while "time-horizon patience" — long the central justification of value investing — is not a genuine edge unless paired with variant perception. The SBF VC episode illustrates how capital mass and network access can substitute for analytical skill in early-stage investing, raising uncomfortable questions about where VC alpha actually originates. Key Points SBF / Cursor / VC Network Effects - SpaceX announced acquisition of Cursor at ~$60B. FTX held an early ~5% stake in Cursor — at that valuation, roughly $2B. SBF also held early stakes in Anthropic and SpaceX; stake sizes for those two are not disclosed in the transcript. - Notably: SpaceX (itself an SBF investment) is the Cursor acquirer — two of his three cited wins are now interlinked, illustrating how VC portfolio companies can compound across one another. - Walker's baseline: VCs spend careers trying to hit one "thousand X" grand slam. SBF hit three (Cursor, Anthropic, SpaceX). The FTX bankruptcy court sold the Cursor position back at cost, forfeiting the gain. - Walker's hypothesis: SBF's capital mass and buzz allowed him to short-circuit the normal VC network flywheel — deal flow that would have required decades to build was bootstrapped through willingness to spray capital. Whether genuine analytical talent was also present is explicitly left unresolved by Walker; he raises the question without answering it. - Structural VC observation: Top-tier VC brand (Kleiner et al.) creates a self-reinforcing loop — brand → deal flow → portfolio company recruiting/customers → better outcomes → stronger brand. Emerging managers get adverse-selected into the deals top firms passed on. AI: Force Multiplier vs. Slop Machine - Walker oscillates and does not resolve: AI as force multiplier for talented people vs. AI as equalizer that floods the zone with low-quality output. - Explicit temporal hedge: current AI failures (e.g., "how many R's in strawberry" — gets it wrong today) are treated as a transient condition , not a structural ceiling. He projects improvement within a five-year window. This modulates confidence in any near-term AI-amplification thesis. - Expert-judgment claim: surface-level AI recommendations can miss situational context (Knicks challenge example — AI says 98% win rate; expert knows it's the wrong moment). Expertise still adds value in high-context decisions. KPMG Hallucination / Brand Moat - KPMG published an AI-usage report containing fabricated citations, including false references to Shell. Quoted article: "Big consultancies such as KPMG and EY are viewed as highly credible. So, their reliance on false information increases the risk of second-hand hallucinations." - Walker's tentative hypothesis: legacy institutional brands may increase in relative value as trusted signal-filters amid AI noise. Framing is exploratory ("I've been wondering") — low conviction, no specific names. - Internal tension Walker does not resolve: the KPMG hallucination incident is evidence against the brand-moat thesis — the trusted institution is the vector for laundering false information, not a safeguard against it. Time Horizon as Edge - Walker formally rejects long time horizon as a standalone edge: "if everyone is playing for a one-year horizon, I'm skeptical that simply dragging your Excel columns out to year five is a real advantage." - Rejected the "diamond hands" corollary: he has never met an investor who genuinely had to sell against their will. The operative point (often omitted in paraphrases): "if you have to sell, it's because the thesis is broken" — the real discipline is thesis clarity, not calendar patience. - Three-year rule: if a position is flat after three years, it's time to reassess conviction (his words: "look in the mirror") — not automatically sell. The rule imposes accountability without prescribing action. Polymarket / Prediction Markets - MicroStrategy resolution: market resolved "no" because the Bitcoin sale disclosure was filed the next morning, even though the sale occurred within the resolution window. Walker understands the operational case for bright-line rules but flags the resulting ambiguity risk. - Manipulation concern: Walker is "surprised" thin Polymarket markets haven't been slammed with $5,000 to move narrative or demoralize political opponents — he flags this as a live, underappreciated risk, not an established event. - Structural diagnosis: reflexivity (market prices influencing real-world behavior) combined with cheap manipulation vectors and opaque resolution rules = material risk to business model credibility. Best Quotes 1. "He hit three: SpaceX, Cursor, and Anthropic." — Andrew Walker Frames SBF's VC record against the baseline of a career spent trying to hit one thousand-X. The convergence (SpaceX buying Cursor) makes the three-hit record structurally unusual even beyond raw returns. 2. "I've been wondering if we are entering a world where legacy brands become more valuable because people are desperate for a 'trusted source' to cut through the AI noise." — Andrew Walker Directly investable hypothesis — AI disruption as a moat-widener for credentialed incumbents, inverting the standard disruption narrative. Held tentatively; the KPMG example cuts against it. 3. The implicit corollary — that the real edge must be variant perception — is not made explicit, leaving a productive gap. 4. title: All-In — Socialists Sweep NYC, China Catches Up in Coding, AI Memory Crunch, Micron's Blowout Quarter
text: All-In Podcast Ep. 278 (Travis Kalanick, Gavin Baker, Chamath Palihapitiya, David Sacks) — Research Memo Thesis Memory — not compute — is Baker's named binding bottleneck for AI scaling, with Micron's entire 2026 HBM supply already sold out and DRAM forecast at 30–40% of hyperscaler capex next year; this view is the highest-conviction, most-verified investment signal in the episode. Simultaneously, Chinese open-source (GLM 5.2) has achieved parity with prior US frontier models on coding and agent benchmarks, and Baker's distillation mechanism explains structurally how that gap closes at near-zero cost — compressing closed-model pricing power as a direct consequence. The political context (DSA's 3-for-3 NYC primary sweep at 26% Polymarket odds) is a measurable shift in AI/tech policy risk that the episode's participants take seriously as a regulatory and social license threat. Key Points Memory is the binding bottleneck. Baker: "Memory is the most important bottleneck. It's foundational to the performance of every AI model. DRAM is probably going to be 30 to 40% of all hyperscaler capex next year." Micron's 2026 HBM supply is entirely sold out; revenue up 4× YoY ($9B → $42B cited by host). Baker adds a notable qualifier: this bottleneck "may give us as a society time to adapt our social contract" — framing the memory constraint as a societal stabilizer, not purely a capex call. This qualifier materially tempers a simple bull framing. GLM 5.2 achieves parity with prior frontier models. 744B parameters, 1M-token context window, MIT license, self-hostable, scoring 51 on the AI Index (highest open-weight score ever). Sacks characterizes it as "right there with the previous frontier models" on coding and agent work — parity with prior-generation, not necessarily current, leaders. The gap is characterized as already achieved at that level, not merely approaching. Distillation is the structural mechanism. Baker explains: API access exposes every reasoning token; those traces feed back into open-weight RL training — a "cheat sheet" that compounds with each frontier model release. Resulting architecture: a "council of LLMs" — Grok for truth, proprietary open-weight model on private data. No single closed model wins; orchestration and on-premise inference become the durable layer. DSA NYC sweep: 3-for-3 at 26% Polymarket odds. Mandani-backed candidates won the 10th, 13th, and 7th districts. Sacks frames the DSA explicitly: "We're using the Democratic Party as a ballot access vehicle, not because we share its goals." Baker characterizes the DSA base as wealthy, downwardly mobile white liberals losing ground with Black and Hispanic voters. Chamath claims "pro-AI groups won, but just barely" — but this statement is internally ambiguous given that the same session frames DSA candidates as anti-Silicon Valley; the claim is unresolved and should not be treated as a clean datapoint. Social media age-gating: intra-coalition split. Chamath (tentative): age-gating under-16 could cut radicalization pipelines DSA candidates exploit. Travis (staked counter, maximum conviction): "I'm a full counter to Chamath on this" — the real function of age-gating is forcing adult deanonymization, creating infrastructure for a "full-scale censorship regime." title: Capital Allocators — She Started With "a Computer and a Phone." Now She Runs $4.5 Billion. – Abigail Wattley
text: Williams College Investment Office — Research Memo Thesis Williams runs a $4.5B endowment with a 5% annual spend rate supporting nearly 60% of the college operating budget — a structural constraint that drives every major portfolio decision, including a 27% hedge fund target that is load-bearing for liquidity and volatility management, not merely a return bet. The office is navigating a live internal contradiction: extended private market hold periods argue for slowing commitment pacing, yet the model is signaling a need to increase buyout commitments — partially as a rebalancing response to a current venture portfolio NAV decline. The most durable takeaway is that this endowment's behavior is driven by spending-rate math, not consensus narrative, and its forward commitments may diverge sharply from the "endowments pulling back from privates" consensus. Key Points Portfolio Structure & Constraints - 5% annual spend rate; endowment supports ~60% of Williams operating budget — the binding constraint behind all liquidity, volatility, and hedge fund decisions - $150M lines of credit maintained as backstop; portfolio is 98–99% invested (1–2% cash), requiring active liquidity planning reviewed weekly - 350 line items across the portfolio (~$12.9M average position size); automated data aggregation has freed material analyst bandwidth previously consumed by Intralinks compilation Hedge Funds - Target allocation: 27% across long/short equity and absolute return, down from a prior 40% level - Rationale is structural, not alpha-based: "If the goal was to put it in a drawer and not spend from it for 10 years, you would do something very differently than if you had to draw 5% from it every year" - Cost evaluation is net of fees; no hurdle or historical net IRRs disclosed Private Markets — Pacing Tension - Venture portfolio is currently experiencing a NAV decline; this is the proximate mechanical driver pushing the buyout commitment model signal higher - Model is generating a step-up signal for buyout commitments even as the team stress-tests scenarios for extended distributions — openly described as "a point of big discussion within the team" - Resolution: 3-year rolling average commitment target rather than annual bucket-filling; model is a guideline, not a mandate - Office does not participate meaningfully in co-investments, direct investments, or secondaries — explicitly acknowledged as a capability gap and potential muscle to build Private Markets — Structural Allocation Shifts - Target allocations to both buyouts and venture increased; rationale is companies staying private longer, with private equity now framed explicitly as the vehicle for capturing equity risk premium - Venture portfolio winners treated as still-compounding; patience is the explicit posture Fixed Income - Investment-grade fixed income: exited entirely in 2019 (asymmetric rate probability reasoning); reintroduced ~one year ago at 1% as a "rainy day" liquidity reserve, down from a historical 10% weight - [Editorial note: Guest says "as rates came off zero" to describe the reintroduction timing; rates left zero in March 2022. The coherent reading is she meant as rates came off their highs — consistent with the Fed cutting cycle beginning late 2024. Timeline is ambiguous in the transcript.] Real Assets - Dedicated oil and gas extraction funds: eliminated entirely - Replacement: power and renewable infrastructure — described as exciting but with candid admission they are "still figuring out what it means to manage that portfolio in today's context" Biotech - New focus area, driven by incoming MDs (Julia and Paul) with pre-existing domain expertise and manager relationships - Building conviction toward biotech-focused managers; explicitly constrained by "not doing too much too quickly" — intention and pipeline, not confirmed capital deployment AI & Technology - Multiple internal working groups across AI themes; no structural commitment made - Current use: LLMs for diligence acceleration (private credit sector research, interview prep, off-sheet reference suggestions) — described by CIO as "not revolutionary, but we're using it and we're excited" - Stated risk: being too slow, not too fast Organizational - 11 investment professionals total; 7 investment people covering global opportunity set - Analyst program since 2010; 150+ students through three programs; ~50% stay in asset management - No co-investments, direct investments, or meaningful secondary participation — acknowledged scale limitation at $4.5B Best Quotes 1. "If the goal was to put it in a drawer and not spend from it for 10 years, you would do something very differently than if you had to draw 5% from it every year. Hedge funds make a lot of sense in that context." — Abigail, CIO, Williams Investment Office Significance: Directly rebuts the consensus fee-drag critique of hedge funds by grounding the allocation in spending-rate mechanics. The 27% target is a liability-matching decision, not an alpha claim — and the logic applies to any institution with a material annual draw obligation. 2. "The model we're working on now is actually telling us we still need to be stepping up commitments in buyouts, which is a point of big discussion within the team." — Abigail Significance: Non-consensus signal at a moment when the public narrative is endowment retrenchment from privates. The step-up signal is partially mechanical (venture NAV decline + pool growth = buyout underweight), but the revealed direction is a lean-in, not a pullback. 3. "We no longer do funds dedicated to the extraction of oil and gas. We're doing things in power and renewable infrastructure, which we're excited about, but we're still figuring out what it means to manage that portfolio in today's context." — Abigail Significance: Hard exit from E&P confirmed; the "still figuring out" candor from a $4.5B CIO is a meaningful signal that underwriting frameworks for renewable infra are immature at the endowment LP

title: The Compound — Too Early to Get Off the Wave | TCAF 248
text: Carson Group on Markets, Fed Opacity & the Bubble Question — Research Memo Thesis Ryan Dietrich and Sonu Varghese of Carson Group (~$60B AUM) argue this bull market is not a bubble — the 2021 bust already reset the cycle, breadth has rotated from Mag 7 to industrials/financials without a drawdown (which they call "fantastically bullish"), and historical base rates suggest meaningful duration remains. The dominant risk is not valuation but regime change: a less communicative Fed creates structural vol uplift, sticky services inflation is real but won't trigger hikes, and semis carry the most crowded positioning in the market against an unresolved cyclical-vs-structural re-rating question. Key Points Bull market structure - This bull market just cracked the eighth-longest since WWII; the prior seven averaged seven years, with the shortest at five years — neither guest uses "early-stage," but the base rates imply significant runway remains (inference) - Even Greenspan's "irrational exuberance" warning in 1996 was followed by an S&P rally of more than 100% over the three subsequent years (Dietrich) - Since February 2024, the market is up 47%; since July (last Carson guest appearance), up 17% (Dietrich) Breadth as the bullish signal - Over the trailing 27 days, the S&P 493 has outperformed the Mag 7 by 18%; since 2018, prior episodes of non-Mag-7 outperformance coincided with deep drawdowns — the current episode without a drawdown is historically anomalous and bullish (Dietrich) - Russell 2000 up 20% YTD; regional banks are "the hottest trade in the market" alongside memory (Dietrich) - On a day when the S&P was down 1.4%, 285 stocks were positive — rotation functioning as a market shock-absorber (Dietrich) No-bubble case: the 2021 reset argument - Apple –30%, Google –44%, Amazon –56%, Nvidia –66%, Netflix –75%, Meta –77%, Ark –80% in the 2021–22 bust; post-crash recovery is normal mean reversion, not new speculative excess (Varghese) - Late-cycle signal: equal-weight consumer staples vs. S&P 500 is at a multi-year low , opposite of the defensive rotation that appeared in late 2021 before that correction (Varghese) - One year ago, Palantir was the consensus "must-own" stock — it is now down 50%; rotation is fast enough to bail out the broad market even as individual crowded names collapse (Varghese) Semiconductor tension - Micron quarterly earnings grew from ~$1B to ~$24B; management guided DRAM/NAND supply-demand tight "beyond 2027" (Varghese) - Despite the earnings story, semis historically priced as cyclicals; multiples have "exploded" as margins hit all-time highs — BofA fund manager survey flags long global semis as the most crowded trade; Varghese explicitly names the binary: "Either the industry has become less cyclical or it's a sign of exuberance" without resolving it - Host stated Micron market cap at $1.3T — unverified by guests; warrants independent confirmation before use Fed and macro - Powell's most recent statement: 130 words, near the fewest outside COVID cuts; Powell has cited Greenspan as an inspiration and wants flexibility to react to high-frequency data without being boxed in by forward guidance (Dietrich) - Core services ex-housing is running hot; Dietrich assesses the Fed has "an inflation problem" but will not hike — an inflationary period is not necessarily bad for stocks unless the Fed becomes aggressively hawkish - For the first time in 26 years, equity supply is net positive (Dietrich) - Carson has trimmed gold added post-March 2023 regional bank crisis, citing rising real yields; Varghese stated "since the war started, gold is down" — the referent war is unstated and the directional claim is counterintuitive; verify independently before use Best Quotes 1. Dietrich on breadth as regime signal "Since 2018, anytime the rest of the market outperformed the 'Mag 7,' the market was in a deep drawdown. Right now, over the last 27 days, the '493' are outperforming the Mag 7 by 18%. The fact that the market is remaining healthy with industrials and regional banks ripping while the Mag 7 gets kicked in—I think that's fantastically bullish." Significance: provides a historically grounded breadth criterion that distinguishes healthy rotation from distribution; directly actionable for sector allocation. 2. Dietrich on the AI trade kill-condition "If we do see sustained rotation for six months—tech flat, healthcare and financials outperforming—then I think the AI trade is done." Significance: a specific, falsifiable monitoring tripwire with a defined time horizon and sector signal — rare precision in a podcast context. 3. Varghese on the semi valuation binary "Historically, semis were priced as a cyclical industry. Over the past year, semi multiples have exploded as margins hit all-time highs. Either the industry has become less cyclical or it's a sign of exuberance. Bank of America's fund manager survey shows long global semis are the most crowded trade." Significance: names the fork explicitly without false resolution; the honest framing of the unresolved tension is the analytically useful content. 4. Dietrich on Greenspan's irrational exuberance as anti-bubble precedent "Back to Greenspan's 'irrational exuberance' in 1996. The S&P went up more than 100% in the three years that followed." Significance: grounds the no-bubble case in historical base rates rather than narrative — even credible valuation warnings have not historically marked the peak. Disagreements & Conviction 1. Is this a bubble? — High conviction, structurally biased Both guests unambiguously say no. The key non-consensus argument: we already had a bubble that popped in 2021 (peak-to-trough drawdowns listed above), so this is a new cycle, not a continuation of excess. Supporting signals: staples relative-performance at multi-year lows, breadth rotation without drawdown, irrational-exuberance historical precedent. Caveat: both guests manage $60B+ at a long-biased advisory — they cannot be publicly bearish; conv

The fund's differentiated access claim — reaching top-tier private AI and defense-tech names — remains the critical unverified assumption; the transcript provides hedged company name-drops, not confirmed positions. Jake was initially skeptical ("GW, you're making a mistake, you're ruining your career") but came around. This is the only reference to Jeff's prior investing track record in the transcript and is the origin story of their partnership. Core fund thesis (distribution cost): Jeff: "If Jake can just live his life and get a bunch of views, and someone else has to light $100 million on fire to get a bunch of views, who do I want to be partners with?" Organic attention is framed as a structural capital-efficiency advantage — not a celebrity vanity argument. AGI-pilled barbell thesis: Jake argues that if intelligence is commoditized through compute, what remains scarce is interpersonal capital — charisma, relationships, "vibes." Creator market consolidation: Jake asserts the top-tier creator cohort is closed: "The brands that have stuck around are me, Mr. Beast, and my brother — there's really no one else." He states the original playbook cannot be replicated starting today. Streaming saturation call: Jake: "I feel like what I was doing on YouTube was the final iteration of [streaming]... it's near its peak." Hedged personal read, not a hard data call. Notes escalating shock content as a saturation signal, not a growth signal, and expresses partial culpability. Personal opportunity-cost floor: Jake states "things now have to be $10–30 million opportunities for me to spend time on them." Transcript context is personal time allocation across all business activities (acting, boxing, endorsements) — inference to apply this as a fund minimum check size. AI-generated content and authentic IP: Jeff argues Jake "gets even more powerful in this era of AI-generated characters because he's a 'real' person." Authentic human IP becomes scarcer, not more substitutable, as synthetic content floods the market. "Invest America" angle: Jeff flags the importance of allowing the next generation to participate in private company ownership. Framing suggests potential policy/product interest in retail access to private markets. NFL and Stanford: Jake disclosed he visited Stanford today and stated a serious aspiration to play slot receiver in the NFL after boxing, potentially via a college route. Jeff — Fund's core investment thesis "If Jake can just live his life and get a bunch of views, and someone else has to light $100 million on fire to get a bunch of views, who do I want to be partners with? A lot of people in the space can have a lot of followers, but not the cash. And cash is king." Significance: Frames the GP structure as a capital-efficiency argument. title: Alpha Exchange — David Dredge, Founder and CIO, Convex Strategies
text: David Dredge / Convex Strategies — Research Memo Thesis Regulatory capital frameworks (Basel I–III, VaR) have created a self-reinforcing global machinery of vol supply by treating high-duration sovereign bonds as zero-risk assets, concentrating uncapitalized tail risk in the "safest" parts of institutional balance sheets — the same structural failure as super-senior CDO tranches in 2006. The passive, price-insensitive bid for bonds that sustained this regime peaked in late 2020; what remains is a system clogged with unrealized losses, a "Hunger Games" of sovereign bond issuance, and Japan — the last large net exporter of global capital — as the most likely trigger for the next systemic event. A disciplined buyer of long convexity, sourced from this structural vol supply and concentrated wherever it is cheapest across asset classes, is the appropriate response. Key Points Vol Supply Machinery - Global vol supply originates from three structural sources: (1) retail-facing auto-callables embedding short deep-OTM puts; (2) regulated institutions using accounting capacity to embed short vol (LDI pension funds levering gilts 5x, insurers selling Bermudan swaptions in callable structures); (3) regulatory distortion via Basel zero-risk-weight treatment of sovereign bonds, which suppresses capital charges and incentivizes leverage. - Since ZIRP and QE in the West, this vol supply machinery — originally concentrated in Asia (Korea, Taiwan, Indonesia) — expanded to include European and US markets. - The monetization of financial repression: high-savings, high-growth Asian countries pegging to the dollar created structured yield-enhancement products (short vol embedded in callable notes) for Korean pension funds, Taiwanese insurers, and corporate treasuries. Convex strips the optionality from this supply to build long convexity books. The Structural Regime Shift: Peak Bond Bid - The passive, price-insensitive bid for bonds — central banks (QE), FX reserve managers, and regulated pension funds booking levered gilts as risk-reducing — peaked at end of 2020. - What remains is a system clogged with unrealized losses that regulated institutions lack the capital to absorb; they cannot buy new issuance at scale, worsening the supply-demand imbalance. - Dredge frames the result as a "Hunger Games of bond issuance": Germany issuing rather than buying French bonds; Japan needing to absorb its own JGBs rather than recycling capital abroad. Every sovereign now competes for the same price-sensitive marginal buyer. Japan as the Critical Variable - Japan has been the largest foreign owner of every major global bond market for 35 years. Its retail deposit base was sold 20-year callable Bermudan swaption structures marketed as one-year deposits — when rates finally moved, the system was forced to buy that vol back at scale. - Dredge explicitly states: "It'll probably be Japan that triggers the next fire." The mechanism is capital flow reversal — Japan transitioning from net exporter to net importer of capital removes the largest price-insensitive marginal buyer from USTs, Gilts, Bunds, and AGB simultaneously. - Unlike other overleveraged sovereigns, Japan's private sector (households and corporates) is a net saver; the leverage is entirely government-side, making internal debt absorption theoretically feasible but contingent on BOJ policy and domestic yield levels. Correlation as the Crash Mechanism - The entire structured-leverage system is built on correlation assumptions; when those assumptions fail, forced deleveraging cascades across books — each deleverager worsens the next firm's correlation, creating the feedback loop that produces crashes. - "The system thinks the safest part of the forest is the part that's gone the longest without a fire, but that's the most dangerous part." - This was observable in LTCM's portfolio (1998) and ahead of the 2007 crisis; the same diagnostic applies today to any instrument with long-quiescent realized vol and embedded regulatory privilege. Cross-Asset Vol Mispricing: Rates vs. Equity - Post-COVID, equity vol (VIX-centric) was not attractively priced; it was not the efficient hedge going into 2022. - Interest rate vol from mid-2020 to late 2021 was at "the lowest volatility and lowest price of vol-of-vol ever in history." That was the correct hedge location. In 2022, when correlation broke, rate vol paid. - Dredge's framework is not directional on rates: "We don't bet on rates going up; we build insurance that says vol-of-vol will go up if rates go up." Topside Equity Vol: Persistent Structural Cheapness - For the past several years, upside (topside) equity vol has been consistently, persistently cheap in Asia and US tech names, driven by auto-callable supply and covered-call ETF flow. - The resulting anomaly: "spot-up, vol-up" dynamics in tech names, contrary to the standard inverse spot-vol relationship. This is a positioning-driven distortion, not a fundamental change in vol structure. - Specific reference: levered ETFs on SK Hynix and Samsung create daily structural vol demand-supply dynamics that dealers must manage — a "fight to the death every day." Monetization Mechanics - The fund's crisis monetization is not passive mark-to-market. When markets crash, the same risk models that made vol-selling appear "safe" suddenly mandate that vol sellers buy it back. Convex actively sells that vol back to the original banking counterparties at elevated prices, recycling the risk back through the system. This is a reflexive amplification mechanism, not simply holding options to expiry. - The fund maintains layered convexity: lower-level convexity monetizable in moderate moves (to partially offset carry cost on extreme-tail positions), plus wing positions for tail events. Operational Discipline: Carry Cannot Be Gamed - "If we get greedy or try to time the market to offset the carry cost, that'll put us out of business."
