title: a16z Podcast — Building an Audience in The AI Era | The a16z Show
text: New Media Playbook for Founders — Research Memo Thesis Legacy media is a permanently adversarial channel for founders — Mark dates the break to 2017 and thinks it will never unwind — making "Go Direct" (owned channels plus allied new-media voices) the only viable communications strategy. In new media, the brand is the person, not the company; this is a structural reversion driven by media decentralization, not a trend. Founders who cannot or will not build a personal media presence carry a structural marketing deficit with a ceiling on their total addressable opportunity. Key Points The 2017 inflection: Mark estimates pre-2017 he had a ~90% chance of telling his story through legacy press; since then, agenda-driven adversarial mode has taken over. He thinks this is permanent — the transcript preserves that epistemic hedge. Two-part new-media playbook: (1) "Go Direct" — own channels plus allied voices; (2) "leveraging new voices and new media." (QA note: the second pillar is explicitly named this in transcript; "long-form conversations" is a description of the landscape, not the labeled pillar.) Person-brand is structurally dominant: The corporate-name abstraction (IBM, GE) was an artifact of 1930s–40s media centralization requiring atomic message compression through three TV networks. As media decentralizes, Ford/Edison-style person-branding reasserts. Is it Palantir or is it Alex? Is it Anduril or is it Palmer? "Outside-in" as the cheat code: Never lead with the product. Attach the company to a large, inherently interesting external narrative. Karp talks about the future of the US military and super-intelligence; Petersen goes on 60 Minutes to explain supply chains are collapsing. Neither needs to say the company name. The mechanism: founder becomes the essential explainer, not a vendor pitching. Fight selection: Respond to a hit piece — it is an audience-building opportunity. Ben cites his NYT Instagram response as his highest-engagement post ever. Do not engage critics with sub-50 followers; that is wasted capital. Deliberate polarization: "You really want people to hate you and you want people to love you, but you don't want to be neutral… If you're big enough that people hate you, that means you did something important." (Mark) Gabi's two failure modes: (1) Over-index on distribution before the message is locked — distribution is a multiplier on message quality, so amplifying a weak message broadcasts that you are uninteresting. (2) Focus on inputs ("we have so much to say") instead of working backwards from outcomes (who do we need to sell to, who do we need to hire). Comms hiring: Old-media training is "opposite world." Do not hire old-media experience; hire obsessive audience-builders and storytellers. Media presence is a learnable skill: Trump in the 1980s was restrained in interviews; he developed the skill over time. It is not innate. Washington data point: Ben notes that senators and staff now cite the Mark Halperin newsletter — a new-media product — as their primary read, not legacy outlets. Best Quotes 1. Ben (Guest 1) — Person-brand as structural moat: "In old media, the brands were the companies. In new media, the brand is the person. Look at SpaceX — they weren't mad at the company, they were mad at Elon. Is it Palantir or is it Alex? Is it Anduril or is it Palmer? The companies that are winning in marketing, the brand is the person. The rule of new media is that it has to be interesting. If you're a founder who hates this, you're at a marketing deficit. You put a ceiling on your whole opportunity." Significance: Frames founder-brand fusion as a structural competitive factor relevant to valuing high-narrative-premium founder-led names (PLTR, Anduril pre-IPO, RKLB, etc.). 2. Mark (Guest 2) — Dating the media break: "Between 1994 and 2017, I felt like 90% of the time I had a chance to tell my story. But since 2017, that agenda-driven mode took over, and I think it will never unwind. Practically, there is no way to get a story you're going to like through traditional media anymore." Significance: A specific, dated, falsifiable structural call. Implies negative press on portfolio companies should be discounted as systematically adversarial signal, not objective reporting. 3. Mark (Guest 2) — Outside-in cheat code: "The most common startup story is 'we're brand new, we have a new product, please try it.' That is the lamest story in the world. It's fake humble, boring, and egocentric. The cheat code is to find something else in the world that is happening that is incredibly interesting, and plug your company into that." Significance: Causal mechanism explaining why Palantir, Flexport, and Anduril punch above their weight on awareness relative to revenue — and a screen for which early-stage companies understand go-to-market. 4. Gabi (Guest 3) — Message before distribution: "Two big mistakes. One, they over-index on distribution and tactics before getting the message right. Distribution is just a multiplier on the message. If the message is uninteresting, you've just amplified that you're uninteresting. Second, they focus on inputs instead of outcomes." Significance: Two-variable framework to evaluate whether a portfolio company's marketing spend is value-creating or value-destroying. Heavy distribution spend without message clarity is a red flag, not a growth signal. Disagreements & Conviction TENSION 1 — Authenticity vs. Strategic Message Control (internal contradiction, unacknowledged) The central thesis is that authentic, unguarded communication wins in new media. Yet the same playbook explicitly teaches founders to "pivot" — answer the question you want to answer, substitute good questions for bad ones, and attach to external macro narratives strategically. Mark calls the pivot "the Jedi knight thing." The host pokes at this: "Which makes it a little unnatural, right?" Mark concedes — "It does" — then moves on. Neither guest surfaces or resolves the tension. Conviction on b

title: Behind the Balance Sheet — James Aitken on why the price of AI will pop, Kevin Warsh, gold and inflation
text: AI as the China Property Boom Analog — Research Memo Thesis AI is the defining secular trend of our lifetimes and the correct posture is to stay long rather than call a top — the frequency of "when does the bubble pop?" questions is itself a contrarian buy signal. The macro consequence of the AI arms race, defense rebuilding, and the democracies' pivot from efficiency to resilience is a structural inflation floor closer to 3% than 2%, implying structurally higher long-end yields. The most underappreciated investable expression is materials/miners (~2% of S&P 500 market cap), which have been systematically defunded by ESG mandates precisely as AI infrastructure creates a durable new demand vector for physical commodities. Key Points AI / Secular Trend - The guest's top client question for nine months: "When does the AI bubble pop?" — Bubbles do not pop while that question is being asked. The acceleration in semis and picks-and-shovels may reflect FOMO-driven catch-up buying, not peak euphoria. - Richard Zeckhauser — cited as one of the world's foremost decision theorists — called AI "the biggest event of my lifetime." The guest treats this as a high-credibility anchor. - Analog: China property boom. The key error is overthinking it and trying to call the top. The correct posture is to understand the size of the opportunity and stay with it. Inflation & Rates - Democracies have collectively chosen resilience over efficiency (AI, defense, national infrastructure). This is inherently inflationary and the supply-side response is insufficient. - Inflation settling closer to 3% than 2% is the base case, not a tail risk. The 2% target is functionally abandoned by political choice, not policy failure. - Long-end bond yields will clear structurally higher than the post-GFC era. At end-2023, 10-year at ~5% and 30-year at ~5.25% did not cause a recession — AI capex was the offsetting force. Whether the recession trigger threshold has shifted higher or is already closer than feared is explicitly unresolved by the guest ("We shall find out"). - Chinese export prices are rising (based on a client's direct factory visits). If confirmed, this removes one of the last structural deflationary forces suppressing Western CPI, compounding the secular inflation thesis. Materials / Commodities - Materials are ~2% of S&P 500 market cap — guest calls it a "1999-style" setup with room to rise. ESG-driven capex starvation was "an act of self-harm"; the median mutual fund is structurally underweight BHP, Rio, Glencore. - Supply is inelastic: it's hard to bring on new capacity now, and it is cheaper to buy existing supply than develop it → M&A bid is coming for producers with existing assets. This is a near-term catalyst independent of commodity price momentum. - Bloom Energy is named explicitly as a picks-and-shovels AI infrastructure play — fuel cells, world cannot get enough, currently US-only. The optionality event: international market access. Caveat: host noted the idea has appeared in public forums (his Substack), implying some alpha decay. - Exit signal: the commodity bull market peaks when the narrative shifts from "cyclical" to "structural." Guest estimates that inflection is 3–4 years away, but provides no data backing for that timeline — treat as inference. Equity Supply Shock (Near-Term) - Two concurrent headwinds: (1) SpaceX, OpenAI, Anthropic IPOs = massive float expansion; (2) AI hyperscalers have shifted from funding capex via cash flow to borrowing — buybacks "slow to a trickle." - Paul Tudor Jones cited on the buyback-driven float reduction that has supported equities; both tailwinds reverse simultaneously. Guest flags summer (year inferred from conversation date: 2026) as the test window for market absorption. Japan - Ministry of Finance behavior: intervened to push dollar-yen from 160 to 155, then Japanese savers resumed selling yen and buying dollars. This is not a regime seeking yen strength — they are managing the floor, not engineering appreciation. - BoJ rate hikes did not trigger institutional repatriation because Japanese banks have no balance sheet hole — they are "minting money" and have no need to bring capital home. - Preferred expression: long yen-denominated equities (Nikkei, Topix) , not a long-yen FX position. Capture earnings upside without needing the currency call to work. Gold - Peaked well above $5,000 post-Ukraine invasion (central bank and family office demand). During the Iran turbulence, Asian central banks sold gold to pay for imports — gold sold off when it was supposed to rally. Guest: "I pay attention when the price diverges from the narrative." - Currently range-bound ~$4,500–4,600. "Stronger hands" quietly accumulating. Next directional catalyst: Fed cutting cycle or sustained USD decline. - Structural implication: gold is behaving as a liquidity reserve for Asian CBs, not a Western portfolio hedge. Its crisis correlation is inverted when stress is geopolitically Asian in origin. China - Jack Ma's rehabilitation was the "starting gun" — Xi is attempting to engineer an equity culture analogous to Japan and South Korea's development. - Clients not enthusiastic about adding China exposure. The marginal dollar opportunity cost argument: if the action is in the US, why allocate to China? Client channel diligence shows Chinese industrial companies raising prices — a specific, ground-level signal, not a macro forecast. - Recent Trump-Beijing visit was a "nothing burger" by design — letting Trump claim a win while China conceded nothing of consequence. New Fed Chair ("Kevin") - Market consensus: political patsy for Trump. Guest's view: "I'd be wary of that." The East Room debut did not confirm the market's fear he was merely a sock puppet. - Agenda: less reliance on models, less forward guidance, tighter communication discipline, structural work on the balance sheet with Bowman and the Treasury Secretary — reviewing regulatory/balance sheet feedback loops for the first time s

title: Monetary Matters — Why the Electrification Supercycle Is Way Bigger Than Data Centers | Chris Semenuk
text: US Reindustrialization & Electrification: Chris Senek / Tema ETFs (RSH, VOLT) — Research Memo Thesis US manufacturing has entered the earliest innings of a cyclical recovery (ISM PMI above 50 for only 3–4 months after the longest contraction in the survey's history) against a durable secular backdrop of reindustrialization — verifiable in order backlogs and a doubling of the US share of global FDI. The investable opportunity has rotated from Phase 1 (large infrastructure, A&D — now at peak valuations) to Phase 2: short-cycle industrial equipment companies inside the factory walls that are trading at trough multiples on trough earnings, with both a cyclical and secular demand driver aligning for the first time in a decade. Key Points Macro / Cycle - ISM PMI just crossed 50 after three consecutive years sub-50 — the longest contraction in the survey's history. Recovery is 3–4 months old; this is early innings. - April industrial production: +1.7% (measurement period — MoM vs. YoY — not specified in transcript; the guest emphasizes rate of change over the absolute level). - Non-residential construction at "unprecedented highs"; this is committed capital, not rhetoric. - 7 million US manufacturing jobs were lost over the last 15 years; those are structurally gone. Recovery is through automation and efficiency equipment, not labor restoration. Reindustrialization Reality Check - Backlogs as proof: Caterpillar >$60B, GE Vernova approaching ~$90B (guest's language: "north of almost $90 billion") — both extending 2–3 years forward, both described as historically unprecedented. - Reindustrialization is not factory relocation from Asia. It is capture of incremental global CapEx: US share of global FDI has risen to >20% from a historical 10–15%. - Structural drivers: China labor cost convergence (from 30–40x cheaper than the US in 2000 to markedly higher today), IP protection costs, logistics/fuel, and supply chain optionality. TCO math now favors US production independently of tariff policy. - Both the Biden (Chips Act, Sullivan doctrine of self-sufficiency) and Trump administrations (tariff mandate) have embedded the policy tailwind — but the guest implies TCO convergence is the durable driver. - Growth sectors: communications equipment, electrical equipment, semiconductors, chemicals, utility equipment. Not textiles or low-skill assembly. Phase 1 → Phase 2 Rotation - Phase 1 winners (large infrastructure, A&D): now at all-time high valuations. Guest is explicit: exit signal. - Phase 2 opportunity: short-cycle equipment stocks inside the factory — fasteners (Fastenal), pneumatics (Parker Hannifin), vacuum/compressed-air (Ingersoll Rand), bearings (Timken), machine vision (Cognex), automation controls (Rockwell, Emerson). These were left behind during the manufacturing recession. - Caterpillar: all three divisions (construction, resource industries, power/energy) growing in unison — historically rare; early-cycle synchrony that lags into sub-tier suppliers. - Valuation approach for these names: standard near-term EPS is uninformative (many haven't grown earnings in years). Guest uses a 3–4 year normalized earnings power framework, with a combination of DCF, price-to-cash-flow, and historical P/E — not a single metric. Trough multiple on trough earnings is the entry signal; he rejects managers who invest on consensus. Electrification - AI is 6–7% of US power consumption; manufacturing is 26%. AI is a demand driver but not the primary one — the market has mis-attributed the electrification trade. - The US has neglected generation and transmission infrastructure for ~30 years. Now facing simultaneous demand pull from manufacturing, transportation electrification, data centers, and IoT. - Grid rebuild bottleneck is skilled labor, not capital. Largest opportunity is in 765 kV high-voltage transmission infrastructure. - Key names: Quanta Services (labor-moat EPC contractor), AEP (built the vast majority of US high-voltage lines), Eaton (grid-to-chip full-stack exposure), NextEra Energy (explicit 8–9% EPS growth + 4% dividend through 2035 — de-risked vs. merchant/nuclear speculation). Best Quotes 1. Backlogs anchor the thesis to verifiable fact "The backlog at Caterpillar is north of $60 billion. The backlog at Vernova is north of almost $90 billion. So, the notion that this is some kind of fantasy that we don't really see on the ground is frankly nonsense." — Chris Senek Significance: Specific, auditable figures that move the reindustrialization debate from narrative to order book. "Almost $90 billion" for Vernova is the guest's precise language — not a clean figure. 2. TCO convergence makes the thesis policy-independent "In 2000, when China entered the WTO, labor costs there were 30-40X cheaper than the US. Those costs have gone up markedly. When you add in fuel prices, the cost of protecting intellectual property 7,000 miles away, and the cost of retooling, the Total Cost of Ownership makes making things in the US much more sense than it did 20 years ago." — Chris Senek Significance: The non-consensus framing — this trade survives a tariff reversal. Directly rebuts the most common bear case. 3. AI is a secondary electrification driver, not the primary one "AI currently represents 6-7% of power consumption in the US, whereas manufacturing is 26%. AI is important, but it's still small compared to the manufacturing driver." — Chris Senek Significance: Directly contradicts the crowded narrative. If correct, electrification plays priced as AI proxies are mispriced — and more durable than a hyperscaler capex cycle would imply. 4. The rotation call, stated plainly "Aerospace and defense also performed well, but those stocks are now trading at all-time high valuations. The opportunity for an investor now is to look at the companies inside the factory walls—the short-cycle equipment stocks that were left behind. These are trading at lower multiples and are troughing in terms of earnings." — Chris Senek Signifi

title: 20VC — Perplexity CEO: Micron Will Be More Valuable Than Meta & How Export Controls Helped Not Hurt China
text: Perplexity / Aravind Srinivas — Research Memo Thesis The AI value stack is shifting from model capability to orchestration and interface ownership: whoever controls the layer that converts model intelligence into high-value output captures durable margin, while pure-play model providers face commoditization as open-source catches frontier. Power — not capital or chips — is the binding three-year constraint on AI capacity expansion, and the companies that own permitted, powered land extract structural scarcity rent. Perplexity's answer engine was always customer acquisition; the real business is agentic deep research, and revenue has more than tripled in 2026 YTD. Key Points Answer engine = lead gen, not the product. Pro/Max subscription revenue comes from deep research and agentic workflows, not search answers. Srinivas frames every early-stage AI product as a funnel into the frontier product layer. Google's AI Mode is a functional copy of Perplexity. Srinivas claims credit for changing Google's core interface — same font, inline citations, bolding, suggested follow-ups — and states it is "still not as good." He frames this as validation, not threat, because the frontier has already moved to agents. Google is specifically behind on coding models. Srinivas says Google "underestimated the importance of coding models, so they are behind the frontier right now" — a distinct, falsifiable, near-term call separate from the interface-copy argument. Chat interface is structurally incompatible with advertising. Top Google advertisers (Amazon, Booking.com, Expedia) depend on exploratory, vibes-based user intent — which flows to Meta/Instagram, not an objective answer engine. Explicitly bearish on a $100–200B ad business for OpenAI. Model commoditization is the central structural risk for AI labs. "If you're just a reseller of tokens, you have no business because the model will get commoditized." Open-source models closing on frontier quality within 12 months is presented as the expected case, not a tail risk. Orchestration is the differentiator; token value per watt per user is the key metric. Perplexity's claim: it orchestrates across models (not just tools/files), which Anthropic and OpenAI cannot do. This multi-model routing is the basis for its efficiency argument. Micron could exceed Meta's market cap in 6–12 months. Grounded in bottleneck logic: HBM is the binding constraint; whatever is the bottleneck commands the price. Phrased deliberately cautiously ("might not be inconceivable"). Power is the three-year bottleneck, and public resistance compounds it. Permitting, land, turbines, cooling — not capital — are the rate-limiters. Srinivas says resistance will "continue and get worse" based on misinformation about data center water/power consumption. Revenue more than tripled since January 2026. Only hard financial datapoint disclosed. No absolute figures given. Local/hybrid compute is the architecture for durable AI without "going bankrupt." Continuously learning local models reduce context-window costs and address privacy; Perplexity positions itself as the orchestrator across local + server. Team of 400 today; maybe 800–1,000 in two years. Argues AI enables multi-billion-dollar companies built with 40 people — capital efficiency thesis for the sector. OpenAI IPO financial readiness questioned — but only off-camera. Host attributes a pre-show comment to Srinivas that OpenAI isn't financially ready for an IPO. Srinivas deflects on-record without confirming or denying. Best Quotes 1. On Google's AI Mode as derivative: "Nobody ever wanted to ship an answer engine at Google. Nobody wanted to tinker with the interface that made them $250 billion a year. And now you look at AI mode, it looks exactly like Perplexity. There's not even any difference—the font, the citations, the specific bolding of inline text, inline hyperlinks, suggested follow-ups. The whole experience is literally looking like Perplexity, except it's still not as good." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Frames Google's AI Mode as defensive imitation, not innovation — and asserts quality inferiority. If accurate, implies sustained execution risk for Alphabet's search transition and an open window at the quality frontier. 2. On chat's structural incompatibility with advertising: "Who's the number one advertiser on Google? Amazon. Number two is Booking.com. Number three or four is Expedia. How do you book your hotels or flights? Do you book it on ChatGPT or Google? [Host: Google.] Exactly. The interface is less about conversations and more about exploration. When the decision-making is subjective and vibes-based, you don't need an objective answer engine. That's why I'm bearish on advertising taking off in the chat interface." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: A mechanistic argument — not a vibe — against the OpenAI advertising bull case. Travel/e-commerce, the two largest Google ad verticals, don't convert in a chat interface. 3. On orchestration as the true value layer: "If you're just a reseller of tokens, you have no business because the model will get commoditized. We differentiate ourselves at Perplexity because we don't just orchestrate across tools and files; we also orchestrate across models. That is the differentiation Anthropic and OpenAI cannot claim. We can increase the token value per watt per user. The most important metric in AI is token value per watt per user." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Names the sector's structural fault line and introduces a metric (token value per watt per user) that reframes how AI infrastructure and application companies should be evaluated. 4. On the Micron/Meta relative value call: "It might not be inconceivable that Micron, the supplier of HBM, might be more valuable than Meta in the next 6 to 12 months." — Aravind Srinivas Significance: Deliberately hedged phrasing, but the bottleneck-rent logic is stated with higher conviction. Directionally actionable as a framework for relative posi

title: Lenny's Podcast — The hidden pattern behind successful products | Mark Pincus (FarmVille, Words with Friends, & more)
text: Life at the Speed of Play (Mark Pincus) — Research Memo Thesis Mark Pincus argues that the modal consumer product failure is a founder skipping to innovation before mastering best-of-breed execution on the current platform — and that reducing launch ambition is the mechanism that produces the most durable outcomes. His "Proven, Better, New" framework operationalizes this discipline. The second non-consensus claim with market relevance: incumbent social platforms have lost their core adrenaline, creating a structural demand gap that will be filled by an AI-native social entrant — a gap the current model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic) are structurally unfit to capture. Key Points "Proven, Better, New" framework — the Zynga product-management engine. "Proven" means best-of-breed on this exact platform, for this exact audience ; if it hasn't been validated there, it doesn't count. "Better" means something 10 out of 10 existing users would actively switch for — not merely a feature the builder finds appealing. "New" is the single novel wrinkle that drives downloads. In Words with Friends , the "new" was social: friends were already present on the Facebook graph. Founder instincts vs. founder ideas: "Your instincts are right 95% of the time; your ideas are wrong 75% of the time." The framework's answer: isolate the directional instinct (the "innovation zone") and test many specific ideas within it rapidly — rather than perfecting one idea over months. Altitude discipline: Starting at 1,000-foot altitude, not 100,000 feet, is what enables eventual scale. Facebook began as a Harvard people-checker. Zynga began as a Facebook poker game — a deliberate reduction in ambition Pincus describes absorbing social stigma for ("no dignity"). He says he is actively relearning this lesson now. "Kill hope before hope kills you": Distinguishes belief (evidence-based conviction) from hope (confidence without basis). The best product makers collect winnings rather than make bets — they already know they have a hit before going wide. Operationally: use AI as a testing machine to run 100 ideas per day rather than one every three months. Onboarding as the gate: Sid Meier's Facebook civilization game is the named case study — dead on arrival because first-time user experience had too many clicks, so his superior game design was never seen. The most junior Zynga PMs understood "proven" onboarding better than the godfather of game design. Incumbent social decay: Characterizes current social platforms as having lost their "adrenaline." People are "proud to not be on Instagram" and are not missing the party. Frames this as a structural gap, not a cyclical dip, and asserts someone will reinvent social for the agentic AI age using the "cocktail party" dynamic — rowdy, socially productive. Notes that current AI assistants (Claude, GPT) are solitary, not social. Management principles: (a) "Make everyone a CEO" — give people a hill and operating freedom so you don't have to manage them; most motivating for owners. (b) "Stay close to the metal" — be in the room if you are the best player at that position; only delegate when you cannot possibly cover all rooms. These two principles coexist in tension without explicit reconciliation. (c) The CEO's primary job is to be right about product and strategy, not to manage well — Pincus attributes this principle to Bezos. Evaluative standard: Pincus's highest ambition for any product is an "internet treasure" — a service people cannot imagine life without. Best Quotes 1. "Your instincts are right 95% of the time. Your ideas are wrong 75% of the time." — Mark Pincus Significance: Anchors the entire framework. High founder conviction + poor idea selection is the modal failure mode; investors should probe whether a founder has iterated on ideas, not just doubled down on conviction. 2. "Even Sid Meier tripped over what the most junior product managers at Zynga understood as the best-of-breed approach to onboarding. Because he didn't do the 'proven' right, his innovation never got seen." — Mark Pincus Significance: The only named, concrete case study in the episode. Establishes that distribution/UX competence beats design pedigree — and that onboarding quality is a leading indicator of retention, not a lagging polish item. 3. "The best product makers are collecting winnings, not making bets. They already know they have a hit; they aren't launching to find out if people like it." — Mark Pincus Significance: Reframes launch as confirmation, not discovery. Consumer companies that describe their launch as a "test" of whether users want the product are signaling weak pre-launch signal — a diligence screen. 4. "Today we're all hanging out on our Claude on our GPT, but there's no cocktail party… figure out how to make it rowdy." — Host (framing Pincus's thesis) Significance: Crystallizes the market gap thesis — current AI assistants are solitary; the social layer of the AI era remains unbuilt. The model providers are not positioned to capture it. Disagreements & Conviction 1. Copying as a founding strategy — high conviction, Thiel-attributed framing Pincus frames copying competitors as obligatory before earning the right to innovate. He explicitly traces the "moral arbitrage" framing to Peter Thiel ("In the Peter Thiel sense, it's almost a moral arbitrage") — he is applying Thiel's insight, not coining it. Conviction is high and experiential: he personally absorbed social stigma building a Facebook poker game at 41 to prove the principle. The Sid Meier example functions as a concrete falsification of the counter-view. 2. Less ambition → more ambitious outcomes — high conviction, non-consensus in practice Directly inverts VC pitch culture's preference for large transformative purpose from day one. Pincus says he is "relearning this lesson right now," confirming it is an active operating principle. Echoes lean startup theory and Jobs's "start with the customer experience," so it is not theoretically

title: Odd Lots — Carmen Li's Plan to Build a Futures Market for Compute | Odd Lots
text: GPU Compute Futures — Research Memo (Odd Lots, Carmen Lee / Silicon Data & Compute Exchange) Thesis GPU compute is in transition from a procurement cost to a hedgeable commodity, with CME-listed financially settled futures set to launch within months. The near-term data contradicts two dominant consensus trades: inference costs are not falling to zero (token prices doubled in ~6 months), and GPU assets are not depreciating rapidly (H100 residual values near par as of last year). The instrument designed to enable hedging carries structural limitations — definitionally ambiguous volatility metrics, basis risk, and a significant index-provider/spot-marketplace conflict of interest — that a PM must price before treating CME GPU futures as a clean hedge. Key Points Market Structure - Carmen Lee is founder/CEO of both Silicon Data (the GPU price index provider; CME settles against this index) and Compute Exchange (a competing GPU spot marketplace) — a dual-hat structure with no firewall or governance controls discussed in the transcript. This conflict is cross-cutting and affects every claim about index integrity below. - GPU futures and options on CME are launching "in a couple of months" pending CFTC approval; financially settled, accessible through standard futures brokers with conventional margin. - OTC forward contracts can be "physically delivered" — but delivery consists of API access to specific configurations, not a wafer. This introduces counterparty credit and SLA performance risk that does not exist in commodity physical delivery. Index Methodology - Silicon Data ingests 150,000+ traded prices daily; total pricing database spans 8 million points from ~200 data sources. The daily ingestion draws from 100+ sources. - Normalization covers CPU, RAM, disk, geolocation, and memory bandwidth. Output is "highly correlated" but not equal to cloud provider prices — basis risk is structural and explicitly acknowledged. - Competing indices show divergent levels and trends. Lee's response: "the market always votes." Index methodology opacity is an unresolved risk; if the CME contract settles to Silicon Data's index and that index diverges materially from actual cloud costs, the futures fail their hedging function. Volatility & Fungibility - Lee cites "20–30% daily volatility" for A100s and H100s. Critical caveat (QA correction): the term "daily volatility" is Lee's phrasing; the transcript does not clarify whether this is daily price-return standard deviation, intraday cross-sectional dispersion, or annualized vol. A true 20–30% daily return vol would annualize to ~315–475% — extreme by any commodity standard and inconsistent with "healthy." The actual metric is ambiguous and should not be used to size hedges without clarification. - Published research (with Jefferson Lab, presented at a GPO conference) shows 38% performance variance for the same GPU chip across providers — the primary fungibility challenge and the strongest evidence for structural basis risk. Spot Price Signals - A100 rental prices up 10–15% in the past three months; B200 prices initially declined post-launch and have since recovered above launch price — both indicating demand/supply is tightening, not loosening. - Price per million tokens (blended input/output, consumption-weighted across 300 models tracked) has doubled since December 1, 2025 to approximately $2.21 — directly contradicting the consensus inference-deflation narrative. GPU Asset Economics - As of last year per Lee's data: second-year H100 residual value ~85 cents on the dollar; third-year ~84 cents. Lee explicitly contrasts this with car depreciation. Temporal caveat (QA correction): this is lagged data from the prior period; given rapid generational GPU turnover, the figure may not reflect current marks. Lee also has a commercial interest in high residual values (she operates a refurbished chip business). - Data center build announcements do not translate to immediate GPU availability; servers, colocation, and fiber are sequential dependencies. This is a specific, unstated pushback on the headline hyperscaler capex narrative. Institutional Participation - Some banks can cross positions internally; Lee wants dedicated compute trading desks but acknowledges GPU trading requires hardware, software, and regional supply/demand expertise — slowing desk formation. - Speculators are needed to provide liquidity, but financial settlement means early open interest will be dominated by directional bets, not hedgers — a standard early-stage commodity pattern. Best Quotes 1. On basis risk and index utility "This price will be highly correlated to the price you pay at a cloud provider. However, it won't be the same, just like basis trading in other commodities. There's a basis risk." — Carmen Lee Significance: The product's primary limitation, stated by its creator. Basis risk is structural, not solvable — PM must model this slippage before using CME futures as a procurement hedge. 2. On fungibility and the 38% variance "We proved there's a 38% performance variance for the same chip." — Carmen Lee Significance: The single most important structural risk to index integrity. An index averaging across a 38% performance spread produces a settlement price that may bear limited relation to any specific buyer's actual compute experience. 3. On token price inflation "The price for a million tokens has doubled since December 1st of last year to about $2.21, which is a mixture of input/output token prices average-weighted by consumption." — Carmen Lee Significance: Specific, dated, consumption-weighted data point directly contradicting the inference-commoditization consensus. Non-consensus in direction and magnitude. 4. On supply-chain friction in announced capacity "It's not that easy to bring any GPU online. You hear about big data center builds, but they don't translate to immediate GPU availability. You need the servers, colocation, and optical fiber. The stars have to be aligned."

title: Excess Returns — The $700 Billion Shift | Andy Constan on What Happens When Buybacks Turn into Issuance
text: Andy Constan (Dampspring) on IPOs, AI Capex, and the Macro Backdrop — Research Memo Thesis A structural $600–700B reversal in net equity supply — from buybacks retiring ~2% of GDP annually to net issuance — is the most actionable signal from this conversation, and it is self-reinforcing: AI capex-driven issuance only works if compute ROI is validated, so every period of AI uncertainty becomes a supply-amplified drawdown for the exact stocks most heavily owned. Beneath this, consumer resilience is load-bearing on asset prices, not income growth, making equity levels a leading indicator for GDP rather than a lagging one. The near-term read is cautiously constructive; the structural setup is fragile on multiple dimensions simultaneously. Key Points IPO Mechanics & SpaceX - SpaceX priced at $135, opened at $150, traded into the $170s on an $85B float — assessed as a well-executed deal because all constituencies (issuer, employees, underwriters, buyers) were satisfied - SpaceX's implied market cap was ~$2T; the IPO represented ~4% of total equity — Constan's load-bearing logic for why giving away a moderate pop is rational: credibility on 4% is worth more than the price difference on that slice alone - Constan's framework for IPO quality: moderate open pop (SpaceX ~11%) = good deal; 100%+ sustained open = bad deal, issuer "is going to be pissed" and loses future deal access. [Inference: the acceptable range sits between those poles; Constan does not specify a precise band.] - The IPO serves the issuer as the first in a series of capital market transactions (M&A currency, employee retention, future equity raises) — single-deal economics are subordinate to long-term market access Net Equity Supply Reversal - 2023–2024: share repurchases ran at ~2% of GDP in annual net share retirement - Looking into 2026: that has flipped; net supply exceeds net retirement — a shift of $600–700B - Driver: AI capex at ~$1T/year forces capital-light companies to become capital-intensive, canceling buybacks, issuing corporate bonds, and issuing common stock - Constan's explicit view: "it won't cause the market to crash" but is "a significant wall of supply"; conditional downside specifically during periods of AI ROI uncertainty AI Productivity: Two Mutually Exclusive Paths - Path A — disinflationary growth: more output for same cost; no job losses; consumers retain purchasing power to buy AI tokens; self-funding cycle; Constan says this "can be extremely healthy" - Path B — displacement: same output at lower cost; requires layoffs; compressed aggregate demand; workers can't buy the tokens their displacement was meant to produce - Critical qualifier from transcript: Constan concedes a near-term productivity boost is already occurring — "all this spending is going into real GDP." His agnosticism is about durability once the tools are fully deployed, not about whether anything is happening now - His explicit statement: "We don't know yet if it's going to be productive" — deliberate non-call on which path dominates long-run Consumer & Macro Backdrop - Economy is "pretty good" — but the composition matters - Labor market stability reflects a flat and static job pool , not active hiring: "you don't lose a lot of jobs" because no one is aggressively adding them either; no mass AI-driven firings yet because cost/reliability unknowns remain - Real wages are not keeping up with real growth — explicit Constan statement - Consumption is supported by dissaving via the wealth effect: high equity prices, solid bond market, supply-constrained housing. "Dissaving can only go so far" — flagged as a finite, not indefinite, mechanism; no near-term crisis visible Fed & Rates - New Fed chair building credibility through inaction — "luxury of not having to do anything right now" - Constan's non-consensus inflation attribution: persistent inflation is partly the Fed's balance sheet mismanagement, not purely demand-side - Expects "years of tweaks, not a massive reduction in one year" on balance sheet normalization; institutional resistance is real - Explicitly: "when the tailwinds of speculative frenzy and AI investment turn, those headwinds can overwhelm — but there's no sign of that right now " July 24 Tariff Binary - Hard deadline: existing tariffs must be legislatively replaced by July 24 or they expire - Constan's view: if oil prices fall (plausible from tariff removal), headline CPI drops but core rises as freed wallet share flows to domestic goods/services — compositional rotation, not aggregate disinflation - He is "paying attention to that" — treats it as a primary near-term monitor Best Quotes "During 2023 and 2024, share repurchases were roughly 2% of GDP in terms of reduction. Now, it's flipped. Based on all the announced IPOs and the fact that share repurchases are being cancelled or decreased, net supply is greater than what is being retired looking into 2026. title: Chit Chat Stocks — This Digital Payments Stock Is Growing 55% And Trades At 11x EBITDA
text: DLO (dLocal) — Research Memo Thesis DLO is a B2B payments infrastructure company that solves the last-mile problem of collecting and disbursing funds across 60+ emerging markets via a single API — a market Stripe and Adyen structurally cannot serve. An ~85% drawdown from a 300× IPO multiple reflects almost entirely multiple compression, not business deterioration: TPV has compounded at 88% since 2016 (78% since 2019 per host; different base years) with six consecutive quarters above 50% YoY growth. At ~$12/share, with $800M net cash reducing effective EV to ~$2.8B, the guest argues the stock is at an inflection point where top-line growth, margin recovery, and multiple expansion can compound simultaneously — though the take-rate floor thesis is the guest's conditional view ("I think"), not an established fact. Key Points Business Model & Moat - Single-API ("One DLO") gateway to 60+ EM markets; operates under local payment institution licenses, not as a bank - 600+ local payment-method integrations, 38 regulatory licenses (16 more in process), onshore banking relationships — accumulated over a decade of first-mover operation; not patentable but practically irreplicable - "Tollbooth" mental model: any global company operating in these markets pays DLO a fee; value is mutual access, not extraction - Dollar-based retention rates of 140–150% (likely NRR; guest's phrasing is "high retention rates") — reflects expansion revenue from existing customers, independent of new acquisition - Recent AZ Finance acquisition extends the network into Nigeria, Ghana, and Kenya; the only named inorganic action in the transcript Growth - TPV: $1.3B in 2019 → $47B now (host cites 78% CAGR from 2019; guest cites 88% CAGR from 2016 — different base years, not a contradiction but flag for independent verification) - Q1 2026: 73% YoY TPV growth; sixth consecutive quarter above 50% - Revenue: $336M, growing 55%; Gross profit: $119M, growing 40% — the spread reflects deliberate pricing compression toward enterprise customers and high-volume local rails (Pix, UPI), not margin collapse - Tier-1 enterprise customers: Amazon, Netflix, Meta named explicitly Valuation - Market cap ~$3.5B; EV ~$2.8B (net cash ~$800M, ~23% of market cap) - Trades ~17× earnings on market cap basis; EV/earnings multiple materially lower given cash balance; ~11× EV/EBITDA per host - Guest's 2030 price target: ~$70 vs. ~$12 today (~6× upside); note $70 is also the prior all-time high — raises anchoring question - Capital-light model; ROIC above 30%; cash conversion above 100%; no debt Management (Post-Muddy Waters) - Pedro Arnt — former Mercado Libre CFO and 24-year company veteran — became CEO; founders stepped aside - CFO: Lopez Perez, formerly American Express and Visa - Board upgrades: Paco Barara (ex-Citibank), Nelson Matos (ex-Google/IBM) - Muddy Waters allegations (TPV discrepancies, undisclosed founder loan) fully investigated by independent audit committee and forensic accountants; concluded unfounded Catalysts & Optionality - Management guided margin expansion for H2 2026 as investment cycle moderates - New products: "Fuse" (BNPL) and stablecoin settlement rails, cross-sold to existing merchants at zero incremental CAC - General Atlantic holds 22%; potential exit pressure could accelerate M&A - Acquisition optionality: Adyen, Stripe, or JP Morgan Payments named as plausible strategic buyers - Four stated engines: top-line growth, margin expansion, multiple re-rating, share buybacks Key Risks - Top-10 customers = 62% of revenue; vertical integration risk (dismissed by guest as "unlikely" — low-conviction defense) - Currency controls or adverse tax rulings in Nigeria, Argentina could impair near-term cash flows - EM e-commerce slowdown could pressure top-line - Competitive pressure from Stripe/Adyen if they prioritize EM buildout (though guest argues they currently don't) - Take-rate compression continues if volume growth fails to compensate Best Quotes 1. On the moat's nature: "You can't replicate what DLO has built simply by writing better code. The business is an accumulation of over 600 local payment method integrations, 38 regulatory licenses with 16 more in process, and strong onshore banking relationships. What it offers isn't patentable, but it's the product of time, effort, and a first-mover advantage—that's one hell of a moat." — Guest Significance: Directly addresses the AI/tech disruption bear case. The moat is regulatory and relational, not algorithmic — license counts are trackable, making this a falsifiable structural durability claim. 2. title: We Study Billionaires — Surviving the AI Bubble: Timeless Lessons for Investors w/ Kyle Grieve (TIP823)
text: Bubbles, Human Nature, and the Framework for Identifying Them — Research Memo Thesis Every bubble follows Kindleberger's five-stage arc (displacement → overtrading → monetary expansion → revulsion → discredit), and the defining error is always the same: investors pull all future cash flows into the present price, leaving zero return for buyers at the top. The S&P 500's 31× P/E is not broad-market excess — it is a concentration artifact of the Magnificent 7; strip those seven names and the index trades at 19×. The real danger is not the label "bubble" but the assumption that 31× is the new structural floor, and the separate risk that AI — however transformative the technology — replicates the Ford trap: pioneers a category, delivers poor investor returns. Key Points S&P 500 valuation is a concentration story, not a broad bubble. As of December 8, 2025: 31× P/E with Mag7 included, 19× without. The host declines to call it a bubble but explicitly warns against treating 31× as a permanent base. The 12-turn premium sits entirely in a handful of names with deep moats — passive index owners are running that concentration risk involuntarily. Bubble definition as operational tool. A bubble is a time distortion : if a $1,000 asset today is still worth ~$1,000 in ten years, it is in a bubble. This reframes detection as a DCF problem — price already reflects the full compounding runway, leaving no return for the buyer. Kindleberger's five stages as the diagnostic framework. Displacement → overtrading → monetary expansion → revulsion → discredit. Applies across centuries: 1847–1857 plank roads (1,388 companies incorporated, promoters promised 10–40% dividends, roads lasted four years), dot-com (NASDAQ at 246× earnings in March 2001, 77% of 1999 IPOs unprofitable), and current candidates. Terminal value distortion as the quantitative tell. Yahoo in 2000 required 18 billion customers to justify its stock price. RCA pre-Depression: P/E expanded from 15× to 285× despite 35% annual net income growth. Strong fundamental growth did not prevent catastrophic multiple compression — the dominant "expensive but growth justifies it" rationalization is explicitly challenged. AI is an "inflection bubble" candidate. Potentially transformative for humankind, but investors can still lose catastrophically. The host's Ford analogy: Ford was the first large car manufacturer but is "not necessarily a good investment today," illustrating that pioneering a technology does not guarantee investor returns. The required analytical discipline: separate the technology, the business, and the valuation. Quantum computing named as a live "tiny bubble." Rigetti Computing cited by name — price appreciation driven by narrative and hope, not fundamentals. Tiny bubbles are not systemic but "can ruin your personal portfolio." Capable of 90%+ drawdowns on individual books without broader market contagion. Institutional career risk is a structural momentum amplifier. Hedge funds face redemptions if they miss high-momentum names. Nvidia named explicitly as the career-risk trigger. This mechanism is not greed — it is rational at the individual level, which is why it persists and why it creates genuine structural momentum irrespective of fundamentals. Insana's five early-warning signals (exit checklist). Money turns tight; fiscal policies are repealed; innovations fail to deliver; economic conditions deteriorate; public participation peaks. Peter Lynch's formulation: when the dentist and the neighbors tell you what to buy, the market is due for a tumble. Benjamin Graham's investing vs. speculating distinction invoked as foundational. Investing = capturing the gap between price and intrinsic value. Speculating = focused purely on price movement. The host explicitly names this as the definitional test for whether an activity is bubble-prone. Fraud concentrates in bubbles; Enron as template. Complexity masked off-balance-sheet debt and fabricated profits. Vigilance is highest-priority precisely when sentiment makes it feel least necessary. Portfolio prescription: default inactivity for high-ROIC compounders. If narrative — not compounding intrinsic value — is the primary driver of price appreciation, sell even a business you like. If the portfolio is full of high-ROIC businesses with reinvestment runway and excellent management, the correct action is to do nothing. Best Quotes Quote 1 "The P/E ratio of the S&P 500 on December 8th, 2025, is 31 times. If I remove the Magnificent 7, it's only 19 times earnings. The index as a whole is just being propped up by a few outperforming businesses that have deep moats." — Host Significance: Dateable, trackable datapoint. The 12-turn gap quantifies concentration risk embedded in passive ownership — a widening spread signals rising index fragility without signaling broad market excess. Quote 2 "Hedge funds control the largest amount of capital; if they miss an opportunity in a high-momentum business like Nvidia, they increase their career risk. If market sentiment remains bullish, they make more fees. Lastly, there is client pressure. If you don't own the high-flyers, you risk losing capital due to redemptions." — Host Significance: Identifies a structural mechanism — not irrational greed — that forces professional capital into overvalued momentum names. Explains why price-insensitive institutional buying extends bubble duration beyond what fundamentals would predict, and why the exit will be simultaneous rather than orderly. Quote 3 "A bubble is a form of time distortion; investors take all future cash flow and cram it into the present." — Host Significance: Operationally useful definition. Reframes bubble detection as a DCF problem: if price already reflects a decade of compounding at optimistic rates, expected forward returns are near zero regardless of whether the underlying company succeeds. Applicable directly as a valuation screen. Quote 4 "RCA, before the Great Depression, saw its P/E multiple explode

title: Yet Another Value — Alex Roepers on two deep-value special situations: $DCH and $NOMD
text: DCH & Nomad Foods — Research Memo Guest: Alex Roers, Atlantic Investment | Host: Andrew Walker, Yet Another Value Podcast Thesis DCH (American Axle + DLE merger, ~$6.32) is a catalyst-driven deep value situation where the market is pricing ICE-supplier pessimism without credit for a credible $300M EBITDA synergy target that represents only ~3% of combined revenue; rough EPS power of ~$1.50 implies a 4x earnings multiple with a board-endorsed PSU structure anchoring management to $12–$22. Nomad Foods (~$10.21, down from $30) is a "paid to wait" frozen food compounder trading below 7x EBITDA with a 7% dividend yield, insider buying at current levels, and a governance structure that does not preclude a PE takeout — but it is explicitly a "show me" story requiring operational execution from a new CEO. Key Points DCH - Formed via merger of American Axle (US) and DLE (formerly GKN Automotive, spun from Melrose Industries in ~2018–2019); ~$11B combined revenue, listed NYSE at ~$6.32 - Atlantic was an activist in GKN in 2018, pushed the aerospace/automotive split, benefited from Melrose's hostile bid, then re-engaged the automotive stub (DLE) in 2023 with the same playbook - Atlantic also holds Aptiv (APTV) and Continental (CON.DE) — guest disclosed this while discussing naming conventions; relevant context for their broader auto-supplier thesis and as a conflict-of-interest disclosure - Synergy target: $300M+ EBITDA; guest breaks down as ~30% SG&A (duplicate officers, public company costs, workforce), remainder from purchasing scale and 170-plant footprint rationalization; 3% of $11B sales framing is the credibility anchor - EPS power: guest cited "being very rough with numbers, $1.50" — this is a directional placeholder, not a modeled estimate - FCF: zero modeled in 2026 due to integration costs; 2027–2028 are the true cash generation years - Leverage: ~3x debt/EBITDA; Atlantic's sequenced playbook is delever to <2.5x first, then push for buybacks - PSU structure (host's pre-call discovery via Feb 3, 2026 8-K, confirmed by Roers): CEO package begins vesting at $12, scales to $22, over a ~3.5-year window — host frames this as the board's own price target range; Roers agreed there is "good alignment of interest" - Return framing: "double or triple in the next year and a half to two years" if synergies execute — guest's words, contingent on execution and macro Nomad Foods (NOMD) - $3.5B revenue, all European frozen food (Birds Eye and equivalent brands); natural compression if stock re-rates to $15–$20 - Insider buying: Noam Gottesman recently purchased a "large number of shares" at ~$10 (named specifically) - New CEO installed (prior CEO departed end of 2024); known headwinds: private label inroads from Aldi, volume pressure, need for marketing/R&D reinvestment - Guest explicitly labels it a "show me" story ; comfort rests on new CEO, insider buying, and dividend floor — not demonstrated operational recovery - M&A optionality: guest frames Nomad as a PE takeout candidate; key governance point — Martin Franklin and associates are key shareholders but do not control the company , removing a structural veto on a sale - European discount: guest de-emphasizes the valuation drag rather than dismissing it; adds geopolitical resolution as an unquantified upside optionality for European multiples broadly Best Quotes 1. It's a $6 stock; if they do a good job with synergies and things go their way economically, you're looking at a double or triple on the stock in the next year and a half to two years." — Alex Roers Anchors the entire DCH thesis: EPS placeholder ($1.50, explicitly rough), current price, and time horizon in a single statement. The "very rough" qualifier is load-bearing — treat this as a directional anchor, not a model output. 2. Synergy credibility framing "This is only 3% of $11 billion in sales. It is very achievable." — Alex Roers Directly addresses the most common bear pushback on merger synergy targets; context-sizes the ask against the revenue base. 3. 2026 is noise — hear it from the horse "We have zero free cash flow modeled for this year due to integration costs. 2027 and 2028 will be the years they really crank out cash." — Alex Roers Explicit signal to ignore 2026 FCF as a thesis data point; sets the clock for when results will matter. 4. Franklin governance point — the overlooked unlock "They don't control the company. They are key shareholders, but I imagine they don't like the price at $10." — Alex Roers Removes the primary structural impediment to a Nomad takeout. Franklin's inability to block a sale is a non-obvious governance point most holders may underweight when assessing M&A optionality. Roers' actual rebuttal: "coming from 1%, he's not going to own a lot more, and if he achieves the stock appreciation we expect, he's aligning the interests pretty well" — i.e., the appreciation itself creates alignment. title: Capital Allocators — Hotel Investing at EOS – Jonathan Wang
text: EOS Investors / Jonathan Wang — Research Memo Thesis Jonathan Wang's edge in hotel investing rests on a data-driven, market-first framework — weighting market selection at 75%+ over asset-level underwriting — built on 40 years of aggregate US hotel demand compounding at ~2%/year with declines only in discrete global shocks. That foundational pillar cracked in 2024 (demand declined without an identifiable macro shock), and simultaneously the US flipped from net travel importer to net exporter post-2019 — two structural breaks Wang explicitly flags as unresolved and underappreciated. Near-term, he sees the most active acquisition environment in years as seller/bank capitulation begins and market-level divergence makes comps unreliable, creating mispricing that rewards his framework's precision. Key Points Analytical Framework - Core thesis: US hotel room demand grew ~2%/yr from 1987–2023, declining only during global shocks (Gulf War, 2001 tech crash, GFC 2008–09, COVID 2020). This was the empirical anchor for treating hotel volatility as mispriced — sellers and lenders capitulate on volatility fears that historically overstated structural risk. - Framework crack (2024): Hotel demand declined last year without an identifiable macro shock. Wang: "I can't say that in absolute terms anymore." The 40-year pillar is now empirically broken; cause unresolved. - Compression charts identify a ~72% occupancy threshold as the inflection point for pricing power: below 72%, no pricing power; above 72%, ~5% rate growth on average. Threshold varies by submarket due to seasonality and supply dynamics. - Market selection weighted at 75%+ vs. asset-level underwriting — Wang argues most hotel investors invert this ratio, over-indexing on idiosyncratic business plans. Four Investment Pillars (stated by Wang as a defined system) 1. Interesting supply-demand dynamics over the short-to-medium term 2. Non-commoditized assets people choose on attributes beyond price 3. Diversified demand drivers across group, business transient, and leisure 4. No excessive leverage that would force bad asset decisions under short-term stress Market Focus - Seven large urban markets (Boston, NYC, DC, Miami, Chicago, SF, LA) plus coastal drive-to resorts (east and west coast), rotated in/out based on supply-demand dynamics. - Notable: never invested in Hawaii despite ongoing evaluation. Deliberately passed on Austin and Nashville — acknowledges others made money there but forecasts supply eventually stays when demand normalizes. - NYC was the best-performing hotel market globally 1987–2007, then the worst 2007–2019 — attributable to supply overhang, not demand collapse. Primary cautionary example of supply risk. - Secondary coastal drive-to markets (Myrtle Beach, Hilton Head, Cape Cod, Delaware coast, Kennebunkport) identified as underowned institutionally; EOS has become a dominant owner in these markets after a 2019 Myrtle Beach acquisition revealed the pattern. Operating Model - Vertically integrated: EOS owns and manages. Currently 45 owned hotels, 60 total managed (including ~15 for third-party sophisticated owners). - Investment team and operations team are co-underwriters from day one. Operations team is majority partner pre-acquisition, minority partner post. Full accountability shared — prevents the classic misalignment where acquisitions teams hand over aggressive proformas to operations teams. - Business plan buckets: (1) physical renovation ($5M–$70M range), (2) operational improvements (revenue strategies, cost cuts, or cost increases to drive revenue). Implementation begins day of takeover. - Deployment pace: in 6 of 9 years since EOS inception (2017), made one or zero investments. Concentrated deployment when conviction is high. Florida Keys Case Study (COVID-era) - EOS has been the most active investor in the Florida Keys since 2011, with approximately 17 total transactions including this deal (Wang's qualifier: "I think"). - COVID signal: when Florida lifted travel restrictions with 50% occupancy caps, Wang observed rates at existing Florida Keys assets exceeding pre-COVID levels at max allowed occupancy — real-time demand data justifying a distressed acquisition. - Seller: developer with full-recourse loan, lender unwilling to extend at zero occupancy. Price was immediately recognized as attractive due to market familiarity. - Value creation levers: (1) de-branded to independent status — cut brand fees, gained revenue flexibility; (2) cordoned off and sold the marina to a marina rollup group; (3) ~$1M landscaping investment to improve competitive separation from road; (4) operational revenue enhancements. Sold hotel to local owner. Two Structural Breaks Wang Flags as Underappreciated 1. 2024 demand decline without macro shock — breaks the foundational 40-year stability rule; no replacement framework offered. 2. US net travel export — US became a net exporter of travel post-2019 (more Americans traveling abroad than inbound foreign visitors). Wang: "Both components of that are negative." Flagged as rarely discussed in public coverage. Business Travel Structural Decline - Wang characterizes the shift to video conferencing as structural, not cyclical: trend was building pre-COVID, accelerated by forced adoption, and has held. Direct negative for urban business-transient hotels. Platform Expansion — Four-Condition Rule Wang states EOS will never launch a new platform unless it satisfies all four conditions: (1) opportunity with decades of tailwinds, (2) uniquely talented best-in-class partner, (3) EOS can be the best or near-best in the strategy, (4) the platform makes existing businesses better. Residential (est. ~3 years ago): Led by Nicole Cerier. Focus on pivoting across residential subsectors as risk-reward evolves — multifamily, senior housing, others.
